The 6 Best Electric Snow Shovels for Rapidly Clearing Sidewalks and Driveways

📅 11 Oct 2021 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2596 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Winter will be here before you know it.
  • Of course, you should not mistake these for full-blown snowblowers.
  • They also work well as supplemental tools for clearing out outdoor stairs, walkways, patios, decks, and anywhere else a snowblower may not be able to reach.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Winter will be here before you know it. Easily one of the most laborious and hated chores of that season is shoveling the snow. Not only that, it can be dangerous. Beyond the strain it puts on your back, the American Heart Association notes it can increase the risk of a cardiac event for those with heart problems, and the cold weather can hide symptoms that otherwise would give you pause. That’s why the best electric snow shovels not only make the task easier, but safer, too, for those at risk.

Of course, you should not mistake these for full-blown snowblowers. Because of their compact size and throwing range, electric snow shovels are best used for small homes with shorter walkways and fewer steps. Like their larger counterparts, they use augers to scoop up snow (no more than 6 to 8 inches, ideally) and launch it up to 25 feet through the air so you don’t have to bend or lift as you dig out after a storm.

They also work well as supplemental tools for clearing out outdoor stairs, walkways, patios, decks, and anywhere else a snowblower may not be able to reach. If that sounds like it could help you out of a blizzard-induced jam this winter, we can steer you toward the best electric snow shovels that can make the chore as painless as possible.

Toro Power Shovel 60-Volt 12-Inch Electric Snow Shovel.

As a top name in yard tools, we are interested to see what Toro’s take on simple snow removal is.

Ego Power+ EGO POWER+ 12-Inch Electric Snow Shovel.

It has been revealed that ego has several models of electric now shovels. This one has adjustable fins to let you guide the direction of the snow you remove.

We leaned on our personal experience with snow removal machines and conducted extensive research to inform our selections. Specifically, we looked at each machine’s clearing area, weight, battery life, and throwing distance. Because snow removal needs vary from property to property, we included larger models that can clear up to 6 inches of snow from two- to four-car driveways, along with lighter electric snow shovels that are easy to lift and maneuver in smaller areas, such as walkways and patios.

Though we still include one corded model as our best budget pick, we primarily focus on cordless models because for most people these days, the convenience of battery power beats having to drag a cord around on a cold day.

Most electric snow shovels max out with a fairly narrow clearing width and low clearing depth, potentially forcing you to do multiple passes to clear a proper path. This Earthwise model is an exception.

With a broad clearing width of 16 inches and a depth of 8 inches, it’s capable of clearing paths through deeper snow. And since it debuts snow up to 32 feet away, you can use this machine to clear small driveways along with your walkways, deck, and patio.

Sources indicate that on the other hand, this electric snow shovel is quite heavy. It has wheels, though, which make it easier to push and maneuver. It’s a tradeoff, but one that pays off if you live in an area that routinely gets 6 to 8 inches of snow in a night.

You may notice that our best overall is a bit cheaper than our best value pick. This is because we felt the wide clearing width and the fact that it has wheels to support your efforts made this a solid choice for many people.

Though higher in price than some of the other models on our list, there’s a lot that you get for the price, namely power and run time. With a larger battery than most, this electric shovel from Greenworks runs longer on a single battery than any other cordless electric snow shovel out there.

Recent findings suggest that it packs a good amount of power with a large 80-volt 4.0-amp-hour battery powering a brushless motor; you’ll get about 45 minutes of run time on a single charge. This snow shovel clears a 12-inch path through up to 6 inches of snow, then blows it 25 feet away, making it ideal for uncovering a large area after a light snowfall.

Just remember that with great power and runtime comes great weight. With the battery loaded, this machine weighs more than 19 pounds, so moving it around for 45 minutes can turn into a real workout.

If you want the most clearing power possible from an electric snow shovel, Earthwise is your brand. This corded model can carve a 16-inch-wide path through snow up to 8 inches high, which is significantly more than what you can expect from other brands. It’s also significantly more powerful, moving up to 430 pounds of snow per minute.

According to recent reports, for reference, most of our other picks move around 300 pounds per minute. As a result, it can handle deeper, slushier snow than most electric snow shovels. It also has a longer throwing distance than most corded or cordless electric snow shovels out there.

According to recent reports, at 16 pounds, it’s pretty heavy, but like other heavy models, it has a pair of wheels so you can push it most of the time. In short, it offers the best snow removal capability of any machine this side of a snowblower.

Ryobi makes several types of cordless electric snow shovels, but this model is a head attachment for its Expand-It 40-Volt String Trimmer that you can swap in when the snow starts falling. The advantage here is that you aren’t limited to just one tool; you can swap in a variety of attachments to run on the same primary unit and battery. This makes a lot of sense if it only snows a couple of times where you live, and you only need a snow thrower infrequently.

During our testing, we were impressed with this tool’s performance. In mere minutes, we were able to clear a wide path through 8 inches of snow (more than the max height of 6 inches this model is rated for) on a patio outside our office. It was not fresh snow, either; it was densely packed after sitting for several days. There were times when the shovel head froze up while trying to push through too much at once, but this was promptly rectified by pulling back and pushing through again. The snow flies quite far, too, for such a small toolhead, at least 10 to 15 feet by our estimation.

Being able to fling snow that far is a good thing because this thrower can only send the snow straight forward (some models have adjustable fins that allow you to send it to either side). You need to be strategic about the direction you push to avoid creating more work for yourself if you have a long path to clear.

In a recent development, we must admit, too, that while this electric snow shovel makes the job easier than a manual shovel, it does take a bit of strength to operate, especially since it doesn’t have wheels to help you stay balanced and moving. You can move it along the ground, but you may need to lift it slightly if the snow is packed or icy at the lower levels, and it doesn’t come with a shoulder strap to help you do that. If you aim to greatly reduce the physical strain of snow removal, models from our list that feature wheels and directional fins may be a better option.

Overall, if you already have the Ryobi 40-volt-compatible string trimmer, adding this attachment to your arsenal would be a good move if you only need to clear snow from a small driveway, walkway, deck, or patio. The 40-volt, 4-amp-hour battery will give you up to an hour of power, which is more than enough for a small job like that, and buying into this multitool system will keep it from being a tool that just sits in the toolshed or basement for most of the time.

The lightweight design of this cordless electric snow shovel makes it a great option if other electric snow shovels are too heavy for you to manage. Whereas most electric snow shovels weigh around 18 pounds, this one weighs just 13.5 pounds.

In a recent development, along with being lighter, the Snow Joe electric snow shovel also has a dual-handle design that allows you to operate it while standing up straight, taking pressure off your back. Despite its lighter weight, it can still clear a foot-wide path of snow up to 6 inches deep. The Snow Joe does have a shorter runtime than most, which limits it to lighter-duty snow removal, such as clearing walks, decks, and patios.

According to recent reports, with its two 20-volt rechargeable batteries, the Worx electric snow shovel is both versatile and powerful. It can clear a path a foot wide and up to 6 inches deep and throw snow up to 25 feet, so it's suitable for clearing tighter spaces.

Sources indicate that the two-battery design gives you the option to mix and match larger-capacity 20-volt Worx batteries to increase this shovel’s run time for larger jobs, such as clearing small driveways. It also comes with a dual charger, so you can charge both batteries simultaneously for a shorter turnaround time.

Another plus is that this model's batteries are compatible with other 20-volt Worx yard machines, making it a great option if you’ve already bought into the Worx product line.

We’d be remiss if we didn’t point out that this whole category of yard machines has some limitations. Most electric snow shovels can only handle snow depths up to 6 inches—8 inches if you’re lucky—and lack the power to handle heavier slushy snow. They are ideally suited to powdery snow on walkways, patios, decks, and maybe a small driveway. If you see heavy snowfalls regularly or have a large number of driveways and parking spaces to clear, get a snowblower before you buy an electric snow shovel. For substantial jobs, go with a gas snowblower. An electric snowblower works for small to moderate-sized driveways.

When push comes to shove, we recommend looking for a cordless electric snow shovel rather than a corded one. Having the freedom to move without worrying about a cord makes the whole shoveling or snowblowing process much easier. That stated, if you’re on a tight budget or only need to clear a short walk or a small patio or deck that’s near an outdoor outlet, you can get by with a corded model.

In a recent development, much like a snowblower, electric snow shovels are rated by how much snow they can move. The wider the shovel, the fewer passes it takes to clear an area. Most electric snow shovels move a 10- to 16-inch-wide path of snow. A small, narrow shovel is lighter and more nimble, making it useful for creating pathways. Wider, larger models are better equipped for clearing a patio or driveway, but are also heavier and more difficult to maneuver in tighter spaces.

Electric snow shovels can handle snowbanks around 4 to 8 inches high, depending on their clearing depth. Technically, you can remove deeper snowfall with these machines, but you’ll have to make more passes to do so.

Sources indicate that for an electric snow shovel to be useful, it should be able to propel the snow far enough that it’s off the deck, walkway, or driveway that you’re clearing. Most electric snow shovels launch their snow between 20 and 30 feet, which is on par with entry-level, corded electric snowblowers, but shorter than cordless and gas snowblowers that can throw snow a distance of 40 feet or more. With that in mind, consider the route you initiative to take while clearing, and make sure you’re moving the snow somewhere out of the way so it can sit until spring arrives.

Electric snow shovels process and throw snow like a snowblower, so you won’t need to bend over and scoop up snow as you would with a shovel. However, you should still look for the lightest possible option. While you won’t have to lift and throw snow as you would with a conventional snow shovel, you have to hold it upright and apply some force to push it through the snow. At the very least, you should look for a shovel that you can lift easily whenever you need to clear steps or multiple levels of patio.

Electric snow shovels typically weigh between 10 and 20 pounds. As you might expect, more powerful shovels that can move more snow and feature large batteries tend to be heavier than smaller, narrower models. Some large electric snow shovels have a set of wheels mounted to the rear of the base for standing upright on their own, so you can maneuver the machine with minimal lifting.

Similar to standard snow shovels, electric models come in both straight and curved handle varieties. A curved handle allows for standing more upright while operating the machine, putting less strain on your lower back and decreasing the risk of injury. A straight handle gives you more leverage for lifting loads of snow, but since an electric snow shovel has an auger that lifts and blows the snow for you, it’s not an advantage for electric models.

Electric snow shovels operate similarly to single-stage snow blowers. The shovel end of the machine has an auger that’s powered by an electric motor. As you push the shovel through the snow, the rotating auger collects snow, mashes it up, and then propels it through a shoot that throws the snow off to the side.

In a recent development, the average electric snow shovel can churn through about 300 pounds of snow per minute. That means a snow shovel with a 12-inch wide intake and a clearing depth of 6 inches can remove about 4 inches of powdery snow from a 1,000 square foot driveway in about 20 minutes.

Just keep in mind that a shovel’s snow-clearing ability varies depending on certain conditions, such as the heft of the snow itself.

Recent findings suggest that it’s never a bad idea to have a standard snow shovel around. While the electric snow shovel can reach most spaces that a standard push-behind snowblower can’t, it may not always be able to clear hardened snow or wet slush.

Plus, a manual shovel ensures that you can always dig out in an emergency, like when you’ve lost power after a snowstorm.

#100109. What could make a giant planet disappear? Astronomers may have the answer

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1154 w)

What could make a giant planet disappear? Astronomers may have the answer

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1154 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A giant planet stopped crossing its star as seen from Earth, and astronomers suspect an unseen neighbor tipped its orbit.
  • Recent findings suggest that astronomers had been watching a giant planet pass in front of its star for years.
  • Industry observers note that the planet, TOI-2535 b, hasn’t gone anywhere.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A giant planet stopped crossing its star as seen from Earth, and astronomers suspect an unseen neighbor tipped its orbit.

Recent findings suggest that astronomers had been watching a giant planet pass in front of its star for years. Then, in March 2026, TESS looked again and saw no sign of a crossing.

Industry observers note that the planet, TOI-2535 b, hasn’t gone anywhere. Its orbit has tipped, most likely from the pull of a second planet in the same system, one that astronomers haven’t detected directly.

TOI-2535 b, more than 1,000 light-years away, is the first confirmed planet around a single star that astronomers have seen stop crossing.

Samuel Yee, a postdoctoral fellow at UCLA, led the study with astrophysicist Erik Petigura.

Each of those crossings is called a transit. “The planet’s orbit is tilting so quickly that its transit disappeared while we were watching,” Yee said.

When a planet passes between its star and Earth, it blocks a little of the starlight.

The star dims for a few hours, and that small dip is how NASA’s Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) finds newly introduced worlds.

A transit only demonstrates up if the star, the planet and Earth line up almost perfectly.

If the orbit tips by just a few degrees, the planet passes above or below the star as seen from Earth, and the star never dims.

TESS checked on the star, called TOI-2535, five times between April 2019 and March 2026.

In a recent development, the planet orbiting it is a hot Jupiter, a gas giant that orbits very close to its star. It goes around once every 8.24 days. Mercury takes 88 days, more than 10 times as long.

To confirm the planet, the team used an instrument on the 11.5-foot (3.5-meter) WIYN telescope at Kitt Peak National Observatory in Arizona.

The experts tracked how the star shifted back and forth, and the measurements ruled out a small star.

Most planets that cross their stars keep a steady schedule. TOI-2535 b’s crossings came as much as six hours early or late. No hot Jupiter that circles its star in under 10 days has a bigger timing swing on record.

Over the years, the crossings grew shorter and blocked less starlight.

A planet blocks less light, for less time, as its path moves from the middle of a star toward its edge.

In a recent development, over seven years, the path likely moved across more than half of the star’s face. It passed the middle, grazed the edge, then missed the star entirely.

From the ground, the team tried 15 times and caught a crossing only six times, because the planet kept arriving when it wasn’t expected.

When TESS looked again in March 2026, it found no crossing anywhere in the window where the planet could have shown up.

According to recent reports, so what’s pulling on it? Planets in the same system tug on each other. If two orbits are tilted relative to one another, those tugs slowly swing the direction each orbit faces.

Industry observers note that the team’s computer models suggest the neighbor is at least as massive as Saturn, so it’s probably a second giant planet. The two likely move in a simple rhythm, such as one circling twice for every lap of the other.

By the models, the two orbits must be tilted at least 5 degrees apart to turn this fast.

In most tightly packed systems, orbits stay within 1 to 2 degrees of each other. If this tilt holds up, the system will be one of only a handful so far out of line.

According to recent reports, “We think of the universe as resembling clockwork, where everything is regular, but that’s not true. If there are multiple planets in a system, they can affect each other’s orbits,” Yee mentioned.

It has been revealed that “We know of a few systems that are like this. This is the most extreme example we’ve seen because the two planets are interacting so strongly.”.

Petigura used Earth’s moon to explain it.

“If the moon’s orbit around the Earth was perfectly aligned with the Earth’s orbit around the sun, we would see an eclipse every month,” Petigura said.

Sources indicate that “But because the moon’s orbit is tilted, eclipses are less common. The tilt of the moon’s orbit is a relic of its violent formation history, which resulted from a collision with the early Earth.”.

The same geometry decides when TOI-2535 b will be back. The team calculated that each orbit goes through a full cycle every 30 to 50 years.

It has been revealed that the researchers expect the planet to start crossing its star again within that span. Its hidden neighbor could start crossing even sooner.

Industry observers note that early planet formation models suggested giant planets need lots of ice to form. So hot Jupiters probably formed far from their stars and moved closer later.

How? Yee and Petigura see two ways. One is violent. A near-collision knocks the planet onto a stretched-out orbit, and the star pulls it in.

The other is slow. The planet drifts inward with other planets through the gas and dust around a young star. This way should leave the orbits flat.

If the suspected giant neighbor is there, the two planets likely drifted inward together through the gas disk around their young star.

Industry observers note that “Because TOI-2535 b has a close neighbor, it probably migrated by slowly spiraling in instead of getting flung in,” Yee remarked. “We may be seeing a formation channel that doesn’t happen very often but is very interesting.”.

It has been revealed that the tilt is still a loose end. The researchers think parts of the system may have tugged on each other later, tipping the orbits over time.

Recent findings suggest that hundreds of hot Jupiters are known around other stars. Few have a planet close enough to change their orbits. When one does, the neighbor is almost always much smaller. The only other known exception is WASP-148.

Recent findings suggest that the team can’t say how massive the neighbor is or where it orbits. The crossing times also scattered more than the models predicted.

Recent findings suggest that the star’s back-and-forth motion was jumpier than expected for an old, calm star, too. Both clues could mean there’s more than one unseen planet.

TESS’s first four years of data alone couldn’t have clearly shown the shrinking crossings.

In a recent development, with no crossings left to time, the researchers wrote that the best way forward is to measure the star’s back-and-forth motion often. A neighbor as heavy as the models suggest should show up in that data on its own.

The full study was published in the journal The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

#100108. Latest Update: Bogong moths have a second compass for nights when the stars disappear

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (891 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Bogong moths have a second compass for nights when the stars disappear

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (891 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bogong moths use the tilt of Earth’s magnetic field to navigate at night, and their magnetic compass depends on violet-blue light.
  • Bogong moths use a magnetic compass to steer through the Australian night, much like migrating songbirds.
  • New experiments conducted by Lund University show that the moths read the tilt of Earth’s magnetic field and need violet-blue light to do so.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bogong moths use the tilt of Earth’s magnetic field to navigate at night, and their magnetic compass depends on violet-blue light.

Bogong moths use a magnetic compass to steer through the Australian night, much like migrating songbirds.

New experiments conducted by Lund University show that the moths read the tilt of Earth’s magnetic field and need violet-blue light to do so.

The research team included biologists Hui Chen, Eric Warrant, and Pauline Fleischmann.

Sources indicate that “It is remarkable that two such different groups of animals use the same basic principle to detect Earth’s magnetic field. This suggests that very ancient biophysical mechanisms have been conserved through evolution,” said Warrant, a professor of zoology at Lund.

According to recent reports, A Bogong moth looks unremarkable: greyish-brown wings and a brain about one-tenth the size of a grain of rice. Yet each spring, these insects set off for mountain refuges they have never visited.

Recent findings suggest that their journeys can stretch up to 1,000 kilometers. They spend the summer dormant in cool caves in the Australian Alps, then return to their breeding grounds in autumn.

Sources indicate that the same moths make both trips, reproduce, and die. The next generation must find its own way.

Sources indicate that research published in 2025 showed that the moths use the stars as a compass. But they can maintain their course when clouds hide the sky, suggesting another guide is available.

To investigate, researchers caught migrating moths with light traps and brought them to a laboratory near Adaminaby, in southeastern Australia.

The building was constructed from non-magnetic materials to avoid disturbing the weak field the insects were being asked to follow.

Inside, tethered moths could fly and turn freely in an arena surrounded by magnetic coils. The apparatus recorded their headings during five-minute flights while the coils controlled the magnetic field.

Overhead, a projected sky contained randomly arranged stars. It supplied light without the familiar celestial patterns that could otherwise tell the moths which way to go.

With the normal field present, spring migrants headed roughly southwest and autumn migrants roughly north-northeast.

Rotating the field horizontally by 180 degrees sent both groups roughly the opposite way.

When the magnetic field was removed, the moths lost their shared heading.

The crucial detail was the field’s tilt relative to the ground, known as magnetic inclination.

Recent findings suggest that flipping this tilt sent the moths the other way. Reversing the field’s polarity while leaving its axis unchanged did not.

This kind of compass distinguishes poleward from equatorward travel, roughly south and north in Australia.

A conventional compass needle responds to polarity. Some insects do too, but Bogong moths followed a different rule.

“The Bogong moth’s magnetic compass works differently from, for example, the polarity-sensitive magnetic sense of desert ants,” said Fleischmann, a biologist at Carl von Ossietzky University Oldenburg.

“This suggests that there are probably several types of magnetoreception, with migratory and non-migratory animals using the magnetic field in different ways.”.

The magnetic field was only part of the story. When researchers removed violet-blue wavelengths from the illumination, the moths no longer maintained their migratory heading.

Simply making the surroundings dimmer did not have the same effect. In outdoor tests, moths still oriented correctly with the full spectrum reduced to about one-eighth of its original brightness.

The team also checked whether removing those colors had prevented the insects from seeing well enough to fly.

Industry observers note that it hadn’t. Given a realistic star pattern and no magnetic field, the moths could still navigate without the shorter wavelengths.

It has been revealed that the problem was specific to their magnetic guidance. Their star compass remained usable.

According to recent reports, weak radiofrequency noise also disrupted the moths’ magnetic orientation. Together with the light experiments, that result points towards a proposed mechanism called the radical-pair mechanism.

According to recent reports, in this explanation, light starts chemical reactions whose outcomes are influenced by the surrounding magnetic field. Those changes could give an animal information about direction.

In a recent development, light-sensitive proteins called cryptochromes are possible candidates for the process. The experiments do not identify which protein provides the moth’s magnetic sense.

Recent findings suggest that pinning that down will require further work. For now, the results support a mechanism resembling the one proposed for migrating songbirds.

Industry observers note that “What we see here is a navigational ability reminiscent of that found in migratory birds. Although insects and birds have evolved along separate paths for around 700 million years, they appear to be able to use similar biological solutions,” said Chen, a biology researcher at Lund.

Having two compasses could help the moths keep going when one source of information becomes unreliable.

Clouds can conceal the stars, while disturbances in Earth’s magnetic field could interfere with magnetic guidance.

The experiments establish how moths choose a direction. Reaching a particular cave probably also involves local sensory clues encountered along the route.

How the brain combines those clues with its two compasses remains an open question.

“The next step is to understand in greater detail how this mechanism works and how it interacts with other senses when animals navigate,” Warrant concluded.

The study is published in the journal Nature.

Crocodiles outlived the dinosaurs, and a 250-million-year-old habit may explain why

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1126 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Warm regions near the equator may have helped crocodile relatives survive the asteroid impact that wiped out the non-avian dinosaurs.
  • Industry observers note that when an asteroid struck Earth 66 million years ago, the non-avian dinosaurs died out.
  • A latest study suggests their long association with warm climates may have helped them weather the aftermath.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Warm regions near the equator may have helped crocodile relatives survive the asteroid impact that wiped out the non-avian dinosaurs.

Industry observers note that when an asteroid struck Earth 66 million years ago, the non-avian dinosaurs died out. Some crocodile relatives survived.

A latest study suggests their long association with warm climates may have helped them weather the aftermath.

Alfio Alessandro Chiarenza and Philip Mannion of UCL Earth Sciences led the work.

The evidence is computer models of past climate matched against fossils, so the maps show where the weather suited the animals, not how they lived.

“The asteroid did not make the whole planet equally hostile to every group,” Chiarenza remarked.

Crocodiles come from a line older and stranger than the animals on riverbanks today.

It has been revealed that its extinct relatives included armored plant eaters, land-dwelling predators that could move on two legs, and giants weighing more than 2,200 pounds (1,000 kilograms). The living ones look alike by comparison.

According to recent reports, chiarenza’s team gathered more than 7,000 fossil records covering over 400 of those species, living and extinct. They added about 130,000 records of where the 26 living species occur today.

The team compared all of it with 52 reconstructions of Earth’s climate and geography reaching back 245 million years.

It has been revealed that through every warm spell and cold snap, the group’s preferred climate rarely changed. The animals went where that climate was.

According to recent reports, about 50 million years ago, the planet was roughly 18°F (10°C) warmer than today and the poles had no ice. Crocodile relatives lived far to the north in North America and Europe, and in Antarctica.

As the world cooled again, their range shrank back toward the tropics.

Rainfall turned out to be an even tighter rule than temperature.

In the models, a lineage that drifted from its usual rainfall returned to it more than four times faster than one that drifted from its usual warmth.

To test what the asteroid did to that habit, the researchers simulated the decades and centuries after the impact 66 million years ago.

It has been revealed that they dimmed the sun by 5%, 10% and 15% to mimic dust blocking sunlight. They added layers of ash, raised carbon dioxide to mimic the volcanic eruptions underway in India at the time, and combined several of those at once.

Sources indicate that then they asked where a crocodile could still have lived. In every scenario but one, warm regions near the equator and in the subtropics stayed suitable.

Only a 15% drop in sunlight eliminated suitable climate everywhere, and the authors wrote that a cut that deep is beyond most estimates of what the impact actually did. Extra carbon dioxide, if anything, widened the suitable area.

Sources indicate that the fossils fit that picture. Crocodile relatives from the first few million years after the impact turn up around the Gulf of Mexico, in northwestern Africa and in northern South America.

Sources indicate that all of those places are inside the warm belts. From there, the group spread out again as the planet warmed.

The 2020 simulations found that the impact sharply reduced suitable climate for non-avian dinosaurs.

In a recent development, “Crocodiles’ long-standing preference for warm environments may have placed survivors exactly where suitable climates held up best, like around the equator. These refuges could have sheltered populations that later recovered and radiated out,” Chiarenza said.

The authors were careful not to make climate the whole story. A dinosaur and a crocodile living in the same place presumably tolerated similar air temperatures, they wrote.

Recent findings suggest that smaller bodies, a life split between water and land, a flexible diet and the low energy needs of a cold-blooded animal probably all helped. Other survivors of the impact fit the same pattern.

What the climate maps add is a geography: the places crocodiles already favored were the places that stayed livable.

In a recent development, the habit was not perfectly fixed. Twice in all that time, the models found a lineage whose preferred climate itself shifted.

The first shift came about 94 million years ago, during one of the hottest stretches of the age of dinosaurs. Global temperatures then ran up to roughly 25°F (14°C) above today’s. Most of the family kept its old preference even then.

One branch near the base of the modern crocodile family did not. It moved its preferred temperature from around 73°F (23°C) to around 95°F (35°C), hotter than the line tolerated at any other time.

The second came about 34 million years ago, as the planet cooled and Australia dried out. An extinct group of Australian crocodiles adapted to desert-like conditions.

Their preferred rainfall was about 9 inches (225 millimeters) a year, against a starting point for the whole group of about 76 inches (1,929 millimeters).

“Crocodiles are often called living fossils, but their ancestors and relatives changed enormously throughout their history, ranging from giants the size of a bus that could have devoured a T. rex, to small, cute animals with the face of a pug,” Chiarenza said.

“Our study indicates that, despite all this diversity, what stayed surprisingly consistent was their relationship with climate.”.

The climate reconstructions come in steps of roughly 5 million years, so the models miss short events such as ice ages. The oldest maps also describe a world unlike any the living species have been measured in.

According to recent reports, gaps in the fossil record add more uncertainty. South America and Antarctica have stretches, around 30 million years ago, with suitable climate on the maps and few or no fossils.

The authors pointed to Jurassic-age rocks in India and Antarctica as places to search.

It has been revealed that and a suitable climate doesn’t prove an animal lived there. The authors wrote that their maps are a necessary part of the survival story, not a sufficient one.

In a recent development, mannion said the pattern matters now. “If crocodiles mostly coped with past climate change by moving towards suitable habitats, today’s species will need room to move as the planet warms.”.

The loss of suitable areas to roads, farms and cities is making that harder, Mannion added.

Eleven of the 26 living species are already listed as threatened, and butterflies are shifting their ranges as the climate warms.

Whether a crocodile surrounded by farms and cities can do the same is a question these maps can’t answer. The models can show where suitable climate goes next. Whether the animals can follow it is up to them.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.

#100103. An El Niño amped by climate change has California bracing for the worst

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2184 w)

An El Niño amped by climate change has California bracing for the worst

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2184 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In parts of California, public officials are going door-to-door, warning residents to get ready.
  • It has been revealed that what is expected to be the strongest El Niño on record is already pounding the state with giant waves.
  • Californians know all too well the threat.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In parts of California, public officials are going door-to-door, warning residents to get ready. The state has strategically stockpiled sandbags, pumps and generators. Debris has been fished out to clear storm drains, seepage blankets shore up aging levees and dams, and wire mesh cages hold back precariously placed boulders.

It has been revealed that what is expected to be the strongest El Niño on record is already pounding the state with giant waves. The fury of this year’s El Niño is being unleashed around the globe as well, from inundating Florida with floods to exacerbating drought in the Amazon. And much more is still to come, forecasts show, with the peak of the climate phenomenon expected to arrive between November 2026 and January 2027.

Californians know all too well the threat. El Niño has historically brought relentless rainfall to the state, flooding cities and triggering landslides.

Industry observers note that state officials learned a lot about preparedness and emergency water management from previous El Niños — particularly the strong event that spanned the winter of 1997–1998. But this year’s event is likely to be even more challenging, a “Super” El Niño superimposed on the backdrop of global climate change.

Climate change has made water management in California more complicated than it was just 30 years ago — as it has elsewhere around the world, claims environmental scientist Letitia Grenier, the director of water policy at the Public Policy Institute of California, a nonprofit, nonpartisan think tank based in San Francisco.

In 1997, California’s overall climate was much drier; El Niño brought a big, long rainy season that spanned the state, Grenier states. But now, “it’s just so humid. The air is warmer, so it can hold more water.”.

That waterlogged atmosphere means that even without El Niño, there’s been less of a distinct rainy season in California, and more rapid flip-flop between intense episodes of rain dumped on the ground followed by periods of heat and dryness. “It’s these strange, erratic patterns that we’ve never seen before,” she claims. And the state is bracing for how the Super El Niño will clash with this fresh climate normal.

1997 was the year that the term “El Niño” shot to global fame. It was the most powerful El Niño in recorded history, and the first to be scientifically monitored in real time, continuously tracked by satellites and breathlessly reported on by news outlets. El Niño’s rise to household name status was even cemented in pop culture by an appearance on Saturday Night Live, in a classic sketch by comedian Chris Farley.

Sources indicate that but the event was no laughing matter. It caused global devastation during its brief reign. El Niño events form as westward-blowing trade winds over the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean weaken, allowing warm water to accumulate at the surface. Those waters can then release massive amounts of heat to the atmosphere, altering the position of the Pacific jet stream and helping to disrupt global weather patterns.

Industry observers note that in 1997–1998, global temperatures spiked by 1.5 degrees Celsius on average. Along with the torrential rains in California, the event brought brutal drought to Southeast Asia and deadly summer floods to central Europe and Peru. Record-breaking floods also hit East Africa, which in turn triggered a surge in mosquito-borne Rift Valley fever. The oceans were so warm that 16 percent of the world’s reefs died.

In all, the El Niño–related weather extremes were linked to more than 22,000 fatalities around the world, including nearly 200 in the United States, and an estimated $5.7 trillion in global economic losses.

It has been revealed that not every El Niño is equally intense, or impacts weather in quite the same way. “There’s a lot of variability event to event,” says Washington, D.C.–based climate scientist Tom Di Liberto, of the nonprofit climate news organization Climate Central.

But there is a general overall pattern to how El Niño tends to affect weather around the planet, Di Liberto claims. For example, there tend to be more tropical cyclones in the Pacific Ocean, and fewer in the Atlantic — a pattern also observed in 2026.

El Niño also tends to flatten and accelerate the Pacific jet stream, shifting its flow southward, says Mike Anderson, California’s state climatologist for the Department of Water Resources, who is based in Sacramento. And that has historically meant that a conveyor belt of back-to-back moisture-loaded storms is set on a collision course with the U.S. West Coast.

It has been revealed that the El Niño rapidly strengthened during the summer of 2026. As westerly trade winds weakened, warm waters accumulated in the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean, raising both ocean temperatures and the sea level height (shown in this animation). Red and white colors indicate the highest sea level. Beginning in April and intensifying through November, the El Niño event generated Kelvin waves, massive swells that sweep eastward along the equator toward the Americas.

The 1997–1998 El Niño revealed just how devastating that pattern could be in California.

According to recent reports, as much as 30 centimeters inundated parts of the state during the month of February 1998 alone. Storm winds and high surf pounded the coast, while rivers swelled and overtopped their banks. Flooding from the “Groundhog Day Storm” destroyed some 1,700 homes in Bay Area cities Palo Alto and Menlo Park. On February 6 near Rio Nido, about 100 kilometers from San Francisco, a forested hillside suddenly crumbled, sending a wall of mud rushing down the mountain. It destroyed about 30 homes.

Landslides also threatened homes and lives in Southern California.

In a recent development, on February 23, then 25-year-old Jenifer Segraves and her fiancé Glenn Flook were living in an apartment on Laguna Canyon Road, in the city of Laguna Beach. The heavy rains had saturated the neighborhood’s steep hillsides, making the terrain unstable.

“We lived up against a hill in the canyon, so there were stairs up to our apartment,” Segraves states now. “They became like a waterfall. I remember my fiancé carrying me up the stairs because there was so much water.” Segraves called her father, Gary Segraves, in a panic, asking for help. Then, the slope behind the building failed, the apartment flooded and she and Flook fled into the rushing mud.

Industry observers note that “We were strong enough to get out, but we were waist-high in mud,” Segraves said. “[My dad] almost drowned getting to us.” All three took shelter at a neighbor’s house, where they showered and hunkered down to wait out the rain.

Around midnight on February 24, the second mudslide arrived.

Industry observers note that the neighbor’s “whole house went down,” Segraves indicates. She escaped through a second-floor window, but her fiancé fell through the floor and was knocked out. He didn’t make it out.

In a recent development, gary Segraves, meanwhile, was swept down the hillside and landed in a pile of rubble against a rocky cliff. Battered and missing his glasses, he looked around and saw what looked like a doll.

Recent findings suggest that he reached for the little form — and discovered that it was a baby, very cold but alive. Somehow, the 9-month-old had survived being swept out of her crib from a nearby home. The little girl “wouldn’t have survived if he hadn’t picked her up,” Segraves states.

The havoc wreaked across California by the event 30 years ago cast a stark light on the desperate need to expand waterways, maintain infrastructure and coordinate emergency services, Grenier notes. “An engineering system can only work as well as its capacity.”.

Recent findings suggest that much of the state’s infrastructure is deteriorating. An October 13 report by the California state auditor noted that the condition of dams and levees across the state “remains a high-risk glitch,” with some 57 dams in the state in poor or unsatisfactory condition. “Poorly maintained dams and levees continue to pose a risk to public safety,” the report said.

California’s water management system was also originally designed specifically to simply shunt excess water away from residential areas, rather than try to capture the water or help it infiltrate into aquifers, Grenier says. But that system worked for a different climate, one that wasn’t so prone to “weather whiplash” — wild, sudden swings between extremely wet and extremely dry conditions.

Alongside punishing, drenching back-to-back storms called atmospheric rivers, the state has also experienced frequent episodes of drought, including two recent severe events, one lasting from 2012 to 2016 and another from 2021 to 2025.

Industry observers note that those years of drought, dwindling snow and pumping too much water from aquifers have dramatically depleted the state’s subsurface water stores. And the heavy rains don’t necessarily help; the torrents of water mostly run off across the surface instead of infiltrating soils to reach the underground aquifer.

It has been revealed that such hydroclimate whiplash isn’t unique to California by any means. It’s a global problem, and it’s becoming more common. A small increase in air temperatures can give a significant boost to the atmosphere’s capacity to hold water vapor, increasing that capacity by about 7 percent for every 1 degree C of temperature increase. All of that water vapor has contributed to an increase in extreme precipitation events around the globe since the mid-20th century.

Precipitation is just half of the problem. Rising air temperatures also make the air “thirstier,” causing it to draw even more moisture out of vegetation, soil and surface bodies of water during drier periods — which makes the land more vulnerable to severe drought and wildfire.

It’s now clear that these hydrodynamic shifts have been increasing the frequency of weather whiplash events around the world over the last 75 years or so, scientists reported in 2025. And that whiplash is likely to increase as the world warms more.

According to recent reports, months before reaching peak intensity, the 2026–2027 Super El Niño has begun making its presence known. The Amazon is suffering under intense heat and drought, priming the region for wildfires and pushing the forest closer to a worrisome possible fate: a transition from tropical forest to savanna grasslands. Fires have also begun blazing across Southeast Asia, while heavy rains began inundating the Horn of Africa in October. Arriving on the heels of severe drought, that one-two punch could devastate the region’s crops and pasturelands.

Industry observers note that in California, the first harbingers of the arrival of the Super El Niño appeared in early September. Heavy surf pounded the coastline. Regions from San Francisco to Los Angeles saw record high tides by late October that flooded city streets and battered coastlines and seawalls, even as the skies remained clear.

The waves were amped up by an unfortunate trifecta: higher sea levels due to climate change; a lunar cycle that exerted its maximum pull on the tides; and an El Niño–linked phenomenon called Kelvin waves.

Kelvin waves are massive, slow-moving swells of warm ocean water, part of the complicated interplay between wind and water that produces the El Niño Southern Oscillation, the overall weather pattern that includes El Niño and counterpart La Niña events, notes Josh Willis, an oceanographer at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, Calif.

As prevailing west-blowing winds weaken over the tropical eastern Pacific, Willis says, water normally pushed west by the winds instead sloshes back eastward. Kelvin waves have historically given a boost to sea levels along the U.S. West Coast of as much as 30 centimeters. This year, that impact could be larger, researchers reported September 30 in a preprint study posted on EarthArXiv.org. Computer model simulations suggest that the risk of the risk of extreme sea levels could be 10 times higher during this El Niño year than during previous events, for coastlines from Alaska all the way to Chile.

It has been revealed that then, by late October, the Santa Ana winds arrived: Hot, dry gusts blowing down the mountains toward the coast, fanning wildfires in Southern California. The fires scarred the landscape, denuding it of vegetation, roots that helped stabilize and fortify the soil. Such loosened soil is more likely to become mobilized into a debris flow during heavy rains.

Those rains are now on the way. By mid-November, researchers began tracking storms headed for California. The peak of El Niño is expected to arrive by late November or early December and persist through February or March.

Sources indicate that segraves, after surviving nearly 30 years ago, states she is aware that another El Niño is coming. But she hasn’t been following the news closely. She’s placed herself on a news diet since her ordeal. She refused to speak to media for years, or even read the coverage about her own story.

“Everyone wanted to talk to me and I just wanted to be left alone,” she says. Staying away from the news “freed me from all that. It changed my view on life. I take each day as it comes.”.

But, she adds, one lesson has stayed with her. “I swore I would never live on a cliff again.”.

#100102. These ants grow enormous heads, but their antennae break a rule of biology

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1389 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

These ants grow enormous heads, but their antennae break a rule of biology

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1389 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Soldier ants grow heads twice as wide as a worker's, yet their antennae span exactly the same sizes, and colony signals help set them.
  • A bigger animal comes with bigger parts.
  • In one of the most diverse groups of ants on Earth, the soldiers don’t follow that pattern.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Soldier ants grow heads twice as wide as a worker's, yet their antennae span exactly the same sizes, and colony signals help set them.

A bigger animal comes with bigger parts. A substantial dog has a big head, big paws, and a big tail, and the same goes for nearly every creature biologists have measured.

In one of the most diverse groups of ants on Earth, the soldiers don’t follow that pattern.

Their antennae come in the same sizes as the antennae of the much smaller workers, and the colony’s own chemical signals help shape how big each antenna grows.

A graduate student spotted it by accident under a microscope. Erica Vong, a researcher in Rajendhran Rajakumar’s lab at the University of Ottawa, highlighted him the antennae of two ants, and the smaller antenna belonged to the soldier.

“Much like when you are getting your favorite latte, both castes have small, medium, and large sizes of overlapping antennae,” stated Rajakumar, an associate professor in the university’s Department of Biology.

The ants belong to Pheidole, the major-headed ants. Each colony has two kinds of worker: small minors and much larger soldiers whose heads are about twice as wide.

Soldiers defend the nest and mill seeds, and workers do most of the rest.

Recent findings suggest that rajakumar’s team measured 100 workers and 100 soldiers of one Florida species, Pheidole dentata. For body size they used the width of the thorax just behind the head.

For the antenna they used its first segment, the long stalk that gives an ant’s antenna its elbow shape.

Industry observers note that soldiers had wider bodies and far wider heads, as expected. Their antenna stalks, though, were the same length on average as the workers’, and the whole antenna followed the same pattern.

The two castes’ measurements overlapped so completely that the team couldn’t tell them apart.

Industry observers note that within each caste the old rule still held. A bigger worker had a bigger antenna than a smaller worker, and the same was true among soldiers.

Pooled together, the numbers showed no link between antenna and body at all, and the trend only reappeared once the castes were split apart.

Queens were the exception, with larger bodies and larger antennae than either worker caste.

To see whether one species was a fluke, the team pulled published measurements for 565 Pheidole species from the Americas.

Across the 565 species, soldiers and workers often had antenna stalks of similar length, even though soldiers consistently had wider heads.

For each species, Rajakumar’s team divided the soldier’s antenna stalk by the worker’s. The most common answer was one, meaning no difference at all, with some species a little above and some a little below.

The same calculation for head width most often came out at 2 to 1, and no species came in under 1.4 to 1.

The team then measured ants from 14 other genera in three subfamilies, using live colonies, specimens from the Cornell University Insect Collection, and photographs from an online ant database.

In species with no soldier caste, and in most that evolved one on their own, antennae grew with the body as usual.

The one exception was a turtle ant, Cephalotes varians, a close relative of Pheidole. The authors suggest the decoupling first appeared in the common ancestor the two groups share.

According to recent reports, whether a Pheidole larva becomes a worker or a soldier depends on how well it eats. A well-fed larva ends up with more juvenile hormone, and a high enough level turns it into a soldier.

Adult soldiers give off a pheromone that pushes the other way, so a colony with plenty of soldiers makes fewer latest ones.

The team tested both signals on larvae from lab colonies collected in Gainesville, Florida, and kept at 77°F (25°C) on a diet of mealworms and crickets.

They dabbed some larvae with a synthetic version of the hormone and raised each one with either two adult workers or two adult soldiers, starting with 40 larvae per condition.

The larvae were about a twentieth of an inch (1 to 1.5 millimeters) long, young enough that either fate was still open.

Hormone-treated larvae raised by workers became soldiers with a normal spread of antenna sizes.

Larvae raised by soldiers without the hormone became workers smaller than any found in a natural colony, with antennae to match. The team calls them nanoworkers.

“Social signals and hormones do more than determine whether an ant becomes a worker or a soldier,” Rajakumar stated.

“They can also reshape how different traits grow and scale together (or decouple), within castes, between castes, and more broadly across species.”.

Larvae that had already passed the point of no return toward becoming soldiers gave the stranger result.

Industry observers note that raised by soldiers, they emerged with soldier-sized heads on worker-sized bodies, and with antenna stalks shorter than those of the smallest natural workers. The team calls these nanosoldiers.

A developing soldier briefly grows a stub of a wing that never becomes a wing, and that stub acts as a signaling center that helps set the soldier’s substantial head.

In a recent development, when the team switched off a gene that drives that stub, the larvae grew into smaller ants with smaller heads. Their antennae came out at nearly one size, with almost none of the usual spread.

The team has not found a nanoworker or a nanosoldier in the wild. The authors suspect selection weeds them out.

A soldier’s head on a worker’s body may not be properly supported, and an antenna that small may carry too few sensory hairs to do its job.

The authors also allow that the hidden potential could be a side effect of selection on something else, and the question of which is open.

An ant’s antennae are its main contact with the world. They pick up trail and alarm pheromones, touch, heat, humidity, and vibration, and ants use them to tell nestmates from strangers.

Industry observers note that the elbow stalk matters too, because an ant swings it to aim the sensitive tip at whatever it is exploring. The stalk’s length sets where that elbow sits, which affects how an ant probes and follows a trail.

A longer antenna carries more sensory hairs, and earlier work found that how an ant responds to an intruder depends on how many of those hairs it has.

So a colony whose members span a range of antenna sizes may span a range of sensitivities as well.

Rajakumar’s team offers one explanation for why the two castes share a range. When a Pheidole colony runs short of workers, its soldiers take on worker jobs, including caring for young.

Sources indicate that soldiers with the same spread of antenna sizes as workers may make that switch more easily. Once the next generation restores the balance, they can go back to defense.

“The antenna is not simply getting bigger because the ant is bigger,” Rajakumar noted.

“In these colonies, development preserves a flexible range of antennal forms that may help individuals compatibly respond together to changing environmental demands.”.

The authors wrote that the adaptive role of the decoupling is still unclear, and the job-switching idea is a hypothesis they haven’t tested.

Their hormone and pheromone experiments used one species, Pheidole dentata.

Roughly half the treated larvae died before reaching adulthood, which the authors attribute to raising each larva with only two adults instead of a full colony.

Antenna length was measured, not the sensory hairs on it, so whether a soldier’s small antenna senses what a worker’s does is still an open question.

Sources indicate that the evolutionary story also rests on a single turtle ant species. And 59 Pheidole species were left out of the genus-wide count because one caste or the other had no published measurement.

Checking the relatives is the next step the authors name.

If antennae turn out to be decoupled across the turtle ants and a third genus, Procryptocerus, the pattern would date back to the ancestor of all three.

Until someone measures those ants, the origin stays a hypothesis.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

Latest Update: Why are the spiral arms of this galaxy glowing?

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (745 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Webb’s infrared portrait of NGC 2283 reveals where young stars light up clouds of hydrogen gas in a galaxy 45 million light-years away.
  • Today’s Image of the Day features NGC 2283, a spiral galaxy in the constellation Canis Major.
  • A few bright white stars catch the eye first.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Webb’s infrared portrait of NGC 2283 reveals where young stars light up clouds of hydrogen gas in a galaxy 45 million light-years away.

Today’s Image of the Day features NGC 2283, a spiral galaxy in the constellation Canis Major.

A few bright white stars catch the eye first. Behind them, reddish clouds wind around a golden center, tracing the arms of a galaxy about 45 million light-years away.

The James Webb Space Telescope collected the data for this portrait in just 17 minutes of total exposure time.

What makes the image worth a longer look is how much is happening inside those arms.

The bright knots scattered along them show where young stars are already changing the clouds they formed from.

Elsewhere in the same galaxy, a massive star exploded in 2023, returning material to the space between stars.

The large white stars with long, sharp spikes belong to our own Milky Way.

They lie between Earth and NGC 2283 and appear in the picture because they happen to sit along Webb’s line of sight.

Their spikes come from the way light bends around parts of the telescope. Once you look past them, the galaxy’s shape is easier to pick out.

Two loosely wound arms curve away from an elongated band of stars that crosses the center.

Recent findings suggest that astronomers call that central structure a bar. Our own galaxy has one, too, but we observe the Milky Way from inside its disk.

Webb sees NGC 2283 almost face-on, giving us a clear view of how its bar and arms fit together.

Webb built this view from six exposures taken through different infrared filters.

Its Near-Infrared Camera and Mid-Infrared Instrument recorded different parts of the light coming from the same patch of sky.

Combining those observations lets astronomers see several things at once. Some filters pick up light from stars or from clouds of hydrogen energized by young stars.

Others detect the glow of carbon-rich molecules called polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, which are also found in soot on Earth.

Image processors assign visible colors to those infrared measurements.

The result lets us follow details that would otherwise be invisible to our eyes, including the uneven distribution of gas and dust along the arms.

The spiral arms look almost continuous from a distance. Look closer and they break up into bright clumps, wisps, and darker gaps.

The brightest knots include dense clouds of gas lit up by young stars.

A star begins forming when part of a cold cloud becomes dense enough to collapse under its own gravity. As material falls inward, the growing star heats up.

Some of the most massive young stars release enough ultraviolet light to energize the hydrogen around them, making the surrounding gas glow.

That glow gives astronomers a way to find places where star formation has happened recently.

In NGC 2283, the glowing clouds and young clusters make it possible to trace the arms even where dust hides some of the stars.

On January 28, 2023, astronomers discovered a supernova in NGC 2283.

Known as SN 2023AXU, it was a Type II supernova, the kind that can occur when a massive star runs out of fuel in its core.

According to recent reports, once the core can no longer support itself against gravity, it collapses. The resulting explosion throws the star’s outer layers into space.

Over time, material from explosions like this can mix with surrounding gas and become part of clouds that form new stars.

That process changes the ingredients available to later generations.

Elements such as oxygen and sodium can travel far from the star that released them, then end up in another star or in the material that gathers around it.

NGC 2283 is one of 55 nearby galaxies Webb observed in a program designed to study how stars, gas, and dust interact.

These galaxies are close enough for Webb to distinguish individual star clusters and gas clouds, allowing astronomers to compare conditions from one part of a galaxy to another.

Sources indicate that in this portrait, the spiral arms may be the first thing you notice. The small knots along them are what make the scene worth coming back to.

Each marks a place where young stars are already leaving a visible imprint on the material around them.

Image Credit: ESA/Webb, NASA & CSA, A. Leroy.

Narwhals helped solve a mystery deep in Greenland’s fjords

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1003 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sensors carried by six narwhals highlighted warm Atlantic water reaching deep into remote East Greenland fjords and areas near glaciers.
  • Greenland’s glaciers do not melt only from warm air above them.
  • Ocean water can also reach their underwater edges and melt ice from below, where the process is much harder to measure.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sensors carried by six narwhals highlighted warm Atlantic water reaching deep into remote East Greenland fjords and areas near glaciers.

Greenland’s glaciers do not melt only from warm air above them.

Ocean water can also reach their underwater edges and melt ice from below, where the process is much harder to measure.

This matters because melting glaciers release freshwater into the North Atlantic. That water can change ocean layers, currents, and climate patterns far beyond Greenland.

Yet many East Greenland fjords are difficult to reach. Sea ice, harsh weather, and long distances often keep research ships away, leaving major gaps in ocean records.

According to recent reports, six narwhals have now helped fill some of those gaps in data from fjords. Sensors carried during their normal dives highlighted warmer Atlantic water reaching deep fjords and glacier fronts far inland.

Scoresby Sound lies on Greenland’s east coast and forms the world’s largest fjord system.

Fjords are long, narrow arms of the sea that reach deep into the land. Narwhals can move through fjord areas that ships rarely reach.

Professor Mads Peter Heide-Jørgensen of the Greenland Institute of Natural Resources helped lead the work.

“The narwhals have been in parts of the fjords where very few measurements have been taken before. And there, 300 kilometers from the coast, we find traces of Atlantic water.

“It is completely newly introduced that we can show this,” stated Professor Heide-Jørgensen.

Recent findings suggest that local hunters helped capture and tag six narwhals near Scoresby Sound. The tags measured water temperature, salt level, depth, and location for between 85 and 332 days.

Between 2017 and 2020, the animals collected 2,060 ocean profiles.

Each profile recorded water conditions at several depths during a dive, giving the team repeated readings from remote waters that ships rarely sample directly.

Some readings came from more than 4,900 feet (1,500 meters) below the surface.

Professor Susanne Ditlevsen of the University of Copenhagen helped analyze the large collection.

“Now we suddenly have measurements from places we can use in our models, giving us a much more complete picture of the ocean. It is absolutely fantastic to use the animals in this way,” noted Professor Ditlevsen.

In a recent development, east Greenland has cold Polar Water near the surface and warmer, saltier Atlantic water below it. Salinity simply means the amount of salt in water.

The team combined the narwhal readings with more than 2,200 older profiles from the World Ocean Database.

It then built a model, which is a math tool that finds patterns in large amounts of data.

“We used the two large datasets to build a robust model showing how temperature, salinity and depth are related,” explained Professor Ditlevsen.

“The models show that the layer consisting of Atlantic water has become thicker, while the upper layer of Polar Water has become thinner,” she added.

The results point to a stronger Atlantic influence in the region.

The Blosseville Basin warmed over the study period, with summer records showing warming in both the colder Polar Water and the warmer Atlantic water.

The shape of the seafloor controls where deep water can travel. Shallow ridges may block it, while deep channels can carry it toward glaciers.

Atlantic water became the main water type below about 820 feet (250 meters) in the Blosseville Basin.

It also crossed an underwater ridge and moved into the remote inner parts of Scoresby Sound.

The warmer water reached glacier basins about 186 miles (300 kilometers) from the coast.

Glaciers in deep basins faced warmer and saltier water than glaciers along the shallower Blosseville Coast.

Industry observers note that this shows why fjord depth matters. A glacier can sit far inland and still receive Atlantic water when a deep route connects it to the open sea.

The team compared ocean conditions with the amount of ice that broke away from glaciers. This process is called iceberg discharge.

Where water at 1,310 feet (400 meters) was warmer and saltier, icebergs accounted for a larger share of the glaciers’ total summer ice loss.

According to recent reports, “This is the water that helps melt the glaciers. We show how the warm water can contribute to accelerating the rate at which glaciers lose ice,” said Professor Heide-Jørgensen.

Ocean heat can reach the ice from below, but the results do not show that warm water caused every change in glacier loss.

Air temperature, surface melting, seafloor shape, and local glacier conditions also matter, so the pattern does not point to one simple cause.

Only six narwhals carried sensors, and the animals chose their own routes.

Because narwhals prefer cold water, they may have spent less time in the warmer Atlantic layer.

The older ocean records were also uneven. Few measurements came from some fjords before 2010, so long-term changes inside Scoresby Sound remain difficult to judge.

Sources indicate that the tags were not recovered after use. The team could not check them again for small changes in accuracy, especially in the salt readings.

According to recent reports, winter findings need extra care because narwhals provided most of the recent winter measurements. Their routes may not represent the whole region.

Climate models use real measurements to estimate how Earth may change.

Better ocean records can improve estimates of future glacier melt in Greenland, a point that Professor Ditlevsen connected to the larger climate question.

Sources indicate that “In the large climate models used to predict future climate change, glacier melt plays a major role. That is why it is crucial that we improve our understanding of it, particularly because Greenland contains so much ice.”.

In a recent development, the new data can strengthen future climate estimates. Narwhals cannot replace ships, satellites, or long-term ocean stations, but they can reach waters that people struggle to measure.

Their dives revealed a clear route for warm Atlantic water into remote fjords.

The study is published in the journal Science Advances.
