💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • According to recent reports, at some point, a hot tub stops feeling like a splurge and starts sounding like a really good idea.
  • If you still aren’t sure about whether or not you think it’s worth the purchase, know that there’s a crop of new hot tubs that can ship right to your door and don’t take too long to set up.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

According to recent reports, at some point, a hot tub stops feeling like a splurge and starts sounding like a really good idea. It’s one of the few backyard upgrades that actually changes how you use your space, whether you’re dealing with sore muscles, trying to carve out a little quiet at the end of the day, or just want a place to hang out that isn’t your couch.

If you still aren’t sure about whether or not you think it’s worth the purchase, know that there’s a crop of new hot tubs that can ship right to your door and don’t take too long to set up. You can get some simple plug-and-play models up and running in an afternoon, elevating your outdoor space from a simple yard to a true getaway spot. Others are closer to a full installation, though the trade-off is typically stronger jets, better insulation, and more built-in features. You also have options like basic inflatables, molded shells, or acrylic spas with lighting, waterfalls, and app controls.

For our recommendations, we focused on how these tubs are built, their lineups of features, and what you’re really getting for the price. Here are the ones worth considering, plus what to know before you commit to this major purchase.

To guide our selections, we leaned on our own experience owning hot tubs and spas, from basic models to custom setups.

In a recent development, we chose hot tubs that range from just under $1,000 for inflatable models to high-end models that nearly mimic showroom-quality tubs. But all are available to buy online. Beyond price, we looked at features, capabilities, and fun extras like speakers and ice buckets. Some are a must, while others are mere perks that can elevate your time in the hot tub—and the price.

Sources indicate that we pored over customer reviews and expert write-ups. We also consulted Jeff Courter, an engineer and former owner of Cache Valley Spas in Logan, Utah, to get his insights on how you should factor price, setup, and features into your decision.

Industry observers note that in a crowded field of plug-and-play spa contenders, the AquaRest DayDream stands out for a long list of relaxing reasons. It’s a legit backyard spa without the headache of professional installation and electrical upgrades, which puts this spa in that sweet spot between bargain shopping and custom installs.

We like that it plugs into a standard outlet but still delivers a surprisingly strong massage thanks to 35 jets. AquaRest says the DayDream uses a Jacuzzi-branded pump—and while that doesn’t make it a Jacuzzi spa, it’s still a solid indicator you’re getting a reputable, name-brand component under the hood.

Sources indicate that there are so many nice extras, like ozone filtration and a lighted waterfall, that make it feel more like a full spa setup than a starter tub. The trade-off is in the materials and power: The roto-molded shell isn’t as luxe as pricier acrylic models, and heating can be slow on 120 volts. There is the option to use a 240-volt setup, if you’ve got the capacity. Given the price and host of features, this hot tub is a great choice for those looking to make a long-term investment.

More: Best Inflatable Hot Tubs for Backyard Bliss.

Sources indicate that if you’re looking for a solid hot tub without overspending, we like the Coleman SaluSpa line. The Sicily AirJet is a great choice within that line because it gives you a larger soaking area, 180 AirJets, and a 314-gallon water capacity without jumping into hard-sided spa pricing. This is still an inflatable model, so it does not have the same insulation, jet pressure, or long-term durability you get from a permanent acrylic spa, but the feature set is strong for the price.

It has been revealed that our family has been using a SaluSpa for several months now, and I find it easy to maintain as well. We especially like that the package includes the pump, cover, chemical floater, two filter cartridges and repair patch, which makes the first setup feel simple and straightforward.

Recent findings suggest that we have found the hot tub is hard to connect to the companion app, but we also have no problem controlling it from the panel and do not find a need for an app. For shoppers looking for a quality inflatable that won’t break the bank and has solid reviews, this is a roomy, feature-heavy pick that feels like a better value than many smaller inflatables.

Recent findings suggest that inflatable hot tubs are a great option for folks who want to relax at home without making a more permanent decision (and investment). If you’re looking for a roomy, tricked-out inflatable hot tub to enhance your wellness, the Intex PureSpa Greywood Deluxe checks quite a few boxes.

In a recent development, with 170 bubble jets, a multifunction heater, filter, blower, and hard water treatment system, this model has more features than many inflatables. With a capacity of 290 gallons and included headrests, there is plenty of room for lounging. If you like the features of this tub, but have less space to work with, there is also a smaller four-person model available.

Industry observers note that we like that—for the price—this hot tub includes a lot of fun extras. In addition to the water treatment and jet specs, there’s also a multicolor LED light system and wireless touch button control panel. There are two headrests, a cover, ground tarp, and storage bag included as well.

We do wish there were more than two headrests for a hot tub advertised for six people, but it’s not a deal breaker. One note: Check your available ground space before ordering, too, as this hot tub has a larger footprint than some other popular models.

This hot tub solves a lot of the issues folks face when seeking a therapeutic experience at home—they may not have the space or ability to upgrade the electrical system.

The hard-sided LifeSmart plugs into a standard outlet, skips complicated installation, and still delivers a solid massage with 13 jets, all in a compact, patio-friendly footprint. If you’re hoping to place this hot tub on an elevated surface, though, it’s important to consult a professional and check the load your deck can bear.

In a recent development, even compact four-person models like this one can weigh over 3,000 pounds when filled with water, which is more than most standard decks can handle without added support. And while it’s listed as a four-seater, many users say it's comfiest with two to three adults.

If aesthetics matter as much as performance, this Comfort hot tub leans into both. The acrylic shell and clean wood-look cabinet design give it a more built-in, high-end vibe than most entry-level spas (which typically have rotomolded, all-in-one shells). We love the details like LED lighting and water features that make the whole experience feel a bit fancy.

Sources indicate that it’s not just about looks, though. With 51 jets and a lounger seat, this tub delivers a more immersive soak than simpler plug-and-play models. The trade-off is in installation. For this model, you’ll need a 240-volt hookup, but that also means those jets will pack a lot of therapeutic power at the end of a long day.

If you want a five-person hot tub that doesn’t require rewiring your backyard, the LifeSmart LS500 keeps things simple. It plugs into a standard outlet, sets up rapidly, and still delivers a comfortable soak with 23 adjustable jets and a lounge seat. We wish there were more, but other features (and price) make up for the lack of bubbles.

It has been revealed that the full-foam insulation and thermal locking cover do a solid job holding heat, which helps keep operating costs in check, and the built-in ozonator cuts down on chemical maintenance. We also like the simple look of this spa, which feels a little high-end for the price bracket. It’s not the most powerful spa in this size range, and heat-up times can be slow, but for an easy, low-hassle setup, it’s a practical upgrade.

According to recent reports, while Bestway’s Toronto was our pick for overall best inflatable hot tub, the foam walls do require some extra setup—the process takes two people several hours to complete. On the other hand, the Hot Springs model fully self-inflates in under five minutes and is truly plug-and-play, making it a great choice for those who are purchasing their first hot tub and are not yet familiar with some of the intricacies involved with setting one up and maintaining it.

Sources indicate that everything you need to set it up is included right in the box, with just a level, dry surface and access to an outlet (without an extension cord) required. Despite the lack of foam inserts, this hot tub is still rated for year-round use with Bestway’s Freeze Shield technology. One caveat: While this tub says it's for four to six people, it's really most practical for just four.

Sources indicate that the DoCred inflatable hot tub delivers solo relaxation without swallowing up a small patio or using a ton of water. Think of it as an outdoor bathtub, perfect for homes with only showers or those with very limited outdoor space. The oval shape actually makes it easier to fully stretch out compared to some two-to-four-person circular models, and the included side table and mat are a nice touch.

A few drawbacks: Because the heater and bubble jets share the same pump and limited electrical power, activating the bubbles pauses the heating function until the massage cycle ends. That just means you’ll need to make sure the tub is at your desired temp before turning on the jets. This tub also isn’t rated for cold-weather use outdoors, so think of it as a fun addition to your warm-weather outdoor vibe.

It has been revealed that there are two main types of hot tubs: plug-and-play models and hardwired spas. When we reached out to Courter, he recommended considering several factors before making a decision about which type of hot tub you should go for.

Recent findings suggest that “The right choice depends less on preference and more on your setup, budget, and how much installation you’re willing to deal with,” says Courter. “There are many things specific to the hot tub being purchased. Things such as whether it is insulated, and what R-value does that insulation have?” R-value measures how well a hot tub’s insulation resists heat loss. The higher the R-value, the better it holds heat, and the less energy it uses to stay warm.

He notes that some hot tubs run on gas, though for this guide we’ve chosen only electric models. Where you live matters, too. “Ambient temperature will play a major part in operational costs,” he indicates. “The longer a hot tub runs, the more expensive it is to maintain.”.

Plug-and-play hot tubs are the easiest way in. Most run on a standard 110-volt outlet, so setup is straightforward. They require no electrician, no buried lines, and no major prep beyond a flat surface.

They’re typically made from molded plastic and are widely available online, which helps keep prices down. There are also some inflatable models on the market for less permanent use.

Industry observers note that the trade-off, however, is performance. These models often have slower heating and less powerful jets compared with higher-end models. Still, for many homes (and especially rentals), this is the most practical option.

Hardwired spas require more planning. These usually run on 240 volts and need professional installation, but they deliver stronger jets, faster heating, and a more refined overall experience.

In a recent development, most hardwired tubs have acrylic shells and insulated cabinets, which improves durability and efficiency. They also cost more upfront (and installation adds to that), but they feel closer to a traditional showroom spa experience.

If you’re worried about party-hosting capabilities, be wary. Capacity numbers can be misleading. A “six-person” tub will rarely feel comfortable with six adults. If you have the space, it’s usually worth sizing up.

Sources indicate that A four-person model works well for one or two people who want room to stretch out, while six- or seven-person tubs are better for families or hosting. If you’re mainly using it for relaxation or hydrotherapy, a smaller tub is easier to maintain, and often more comfortable day to day.

In a recent development, take time to think about jet count, but that’s not always a straightforward metric on which to judge a hot tub. What matters just as much is the placement, variety, and adjustability of those jets. Higher-powered pumps will provide stronger flow, as well. A lounger with carefully placed jets is a must if you’re seeking physical relief for aches and pains.

Industry observers note that it’s fun to have perks like lights and sound systems, but those matter less than the features that keep a hot tub up and running for years. A good cover in particular makes a major difference. It helps retain heat, reduce energy use, and keep maintenance manageable.

But once you’ve chosen the size and key mechanical specs that meet your needs, it’s okay to jazz up the experience a bit with neat extras like waterfalls and lights. Just be mindful of additional maintenance. It’s easier to buy a new portable Bluetooth speaker than it is to repair one integrated into a hot tub.

Recent findings suggest that courter said that the exact operational cost is hard to guesstimate—a lot of factors come into play. “The longer a hot tub runs, the more expensive it is to maintain,” he says. “In Northern Utah, we can get down to minus 10 degrees Fahrenheit in the wintertime. In that same timeframe, the average temperature in Miami is going to be in the mid-70s. A hot tub in northern Utah is going to need to run much more often to maintain its temperature.”.

In a recent development, when it comes to chemicals and cost, that also varies depending on the size of the hot tub and how often you use it. General online user reports vary between $40 and $100 a month, but it’s not a number that’s easy to estimate. The initial setup will cost a bit more as you invest in the chemicals and supplies you’ll regularly need.

Industry observers note that while hot tubs certainly are not a set-it-and-forget-it luxury, they are easier to maintain than a pool—and upkeep should not be a major deterrent. “Maintenance of a hot tub isn’t too bad if you stay on top of it,” says Courter. “Usually, it takes 10 to 20 minutes once a week to adjust your chemicals and clean your filters.”.

When it comes to chemical options, whether you choose chlorine, bromine, copper, a salt system, or an ozone generator, they all work just fine—as long as you keep your pH in line. “A pH of 7 on the pH scale is neutral, but the pH of a human eye is 7.5, so I always suggest to my customers that they aim for around 7.5,” says Courter.

According to recent reports, other maintenance will involve keeping an eye on the water level, the condition of the hardware, and any signs of malfunction. Some hot tub repairs are simple and you can even DIY them, but many require calling an expert.

Other than structural considerations if you want it on an elevated deck, the options are virtually endless.

“A factory-built hot tub can go just about anywhere, as long as whatever you are putting it on can hold the weight,” notes Courter. “A dry hot tub can weigh around 1,000 pounds, but remember that water weighs 8.34 pounds per gallon.” That means an average-sized spa could weigh nearly two tons.

Sources indicate that when it comes to ground placement, a flat and level surface with a good base is fine for most uses. If you do choose to place a plug-and-play spa inside your home, be prepared to consult an expert about ways to mitigate moisture damage.

Recent findings suggest that this is another one of those tricky metrics to guesstimate. We’ve listed the warranty windows for each tub we’ve included, but these spas should last longer than that.

“As with most items, it really depends on the quality of the product you buy,” indicates Courter. He says not all hot tubs are created equal and that consumer research goes a long way. That being stated, spending more doesn’t guarantee a longer life for the hot tub.

“If a customer buys the highest-quality tub on the market and doesn't take care of it, it will fail quickly,” says Courter. “I have seen many hot tubs fail in just a couple of years if not maintained the way they should. In contrast, my wife and I still use a Watkins Hot Springs that is over 25 years old. Moral of the story: Buy the best quality that you can and take care of it.”.

A global study maps 45 threats to 21,490 freshwater species and reveals where conservation aims based on land wildlife can miss areas of high risk.

Rivers, lakes and wetlands are home to nearly a third of all known vertebrate species.

A latest global study maps where 45 human pressures, from crop farming to dam construction, are most likely to affect freshwater wildlife.

A team led from McGill University analyzed 21,490 species and found that freshwater threat hotspots often differ from those on land.

For the threats compared, freshwater mammals generally faced greater pressure than land mammals, with a smaller gap for reptiles.

Christophe Brabant, a doctoral student in biology at McGill University, led the work with biology professor Lars Lønsmann Iversen, a member of McGill’s Bieler School of Environment.

The researchers drew on expert assessments to identify the threats facing each species.

They combined those assessments with species’ known ranges to map where the threats are most likely to affect them.

The researchers identified three threats that were especially widespread.

Across river sub-basins worldwide, they estimated that each affected roughly one in four freshwater species present, on average. Farmland growing crops came first.

Dams and other water management came second, and runoff from farms and forestry third.

Industry observers note that europe and northwestern Africa’s Maghreb region carry the heaviest combined load of all 45 threats. In Europe, the dominant problem is pollution from cities, farms and industry.

Sources indicate that in the Maghreb it is pollution plus dams and heavy water use. Other hot spots include the Nile, the Niger Delta and the Rift Valley lakes of East Africa.

The lightest loads are where few people live, in Siberia and northern Canada, and in the Sahara, Arabian and Australian deserts.

Sources indicate that global averages hide massive differences between animals. Fish are mainly hit by fishing across 37% of their range and by dams across another 30.5%.

Farming was the leading threat across 45.8% of amphibians’ combined range and 31.45% of the combined range of dragonflies and damselflies.

The authors linked this pattern to the animals’ reliance on both land and water at different stages of life.

Industry observers note that freshwater reptiles and mammals face a different enemy. Hunting and other direct use are the main threat across 37.8% of reptile ranges and 43.4% of mammal ranges.

That covers the wildlife trade, traditional medicine, animals caught in fishing gear and animals killed on purpose.

In an interview with Earth.com, Brabant noted that dams, farmland, and farm pollution are widespread, but their weight changes from region to region and group to group.

“This means there is no one-size-fits-all approach to freshwater conservation,” he said.

The raw material was the Red List kept by the International Union for Conservation of Nature, which records for each assessed species the threats experts have seen affecting it.

The team took five groups that have been assessed in full: amphibians, fish, mammals, reptiles, and the dragonflies and damselflies.

For each species, they combined its range map with its threat list.

“By combining this data, we could calculate, for any sub-watershed, the probability that a species occurring there is affected by a particular threat,” Brabant noted.

One map per threat per group made 225 maps, which the team stacked into a single index of combined pressure.

Species with small ranges were given more weight.

A threat recorded for a species found in one lake can be placed on the map with confidence, while one recorded for a species spread across a continent can’t.

To test whether the maps mean anything for survival, the team compared them with two separate records.

In the 5% of river basins where extinction risk is modeled to be highest, 71% of the 45 threats were more likely to affect a species than their global average.

The second record was the Living Planet Index, which tracks counts of individual animal populations over time.

Across 2,568 freshwater vertebrate populations from 600 species, populations were shrinking faster in basins with a heavier combined threat load.

Neither record was used to build the maps, so the match is not circular.

The authors wrote that it suggests the maps capture where threats are already pushing freshwater species toward decline.

The study also lined up the freshwater maps against earlier ones made the same way for land vertebrates.

For all seven threats that had been mapped on land, freshwater mammals were more likely to be affected than land mammals.

Freshwater reptiles revealed the same pattern with a smaller gap, which the authors put down to the time reptiles still spend on land.

Industry observers note that the hot spots were in different places, too. Where freshwater fish and frogs are under the most pressure is not where land vertebrates are.

“What surprised me most was how different the geography was,” Brabant told Earth.com. Conservation planning has often relied on information about land species, he mentioned.

That is why freshwater species and their threats need to be written into aims explicitly if the plans are going to reach them.

The Red List treats each threat as if it acted alone, and the authors wrote that many of them combine in ways that could make the damage worse.

It has been revealed that the maps estimate how likely species are to be affected in each area. They don’t measure how much harm each threat causes.

Range maps describe where species live today, so places a threat has already emptied may not show up.

Asked which places he would look at first, Brabant said threat alone isn’t enough. Europe and northwestern Africa lead on accumulated threats, while many tropical regions stand out for the number of species affected.

“Areas of high richness and high threat suggest that threat mitigation is most urgent, whereas areas of high richness and low threats would be most suitable for proactive protection,” he noted.

Sources indicate that what would help most right now, he noted, is reducing the pressures: cleaner water, protected habitat and rivers reconnected. But the most useful action depends on the place and the species.

The next step is matching each basin’s threats to the conservation actions that address them, which the maps alone can’t do yet.

The full study was published in the journal Science.

A group of incoming members of Congress and staff arrive on Capitol Hill for fresh member orientation on Monday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

What happens when more than 100 members-elect descend on Capitol Hill a week after Election Day?

As Rep.-elect Dan Koh, D-Mass., put it, “It really is like high school — but it’s fun high school.”.

Trainings and guest speakers aren’t everyone’s idea of a fun time, but Democrats are feeling good about this year’s latest member orientation. Giddy, even.

The incoming freshmen will pose for a class photo on the House steps. They’ll test their luck in a lottery to see who lands the best office space. And everywhere they look, they see signs of the blue wave that swept over the country.

“I think — well, I hope — that we will be doing a lot of exceeding expectations in this caucus. The American people deserve it and expect it,” remarked Rep.-elect Sam Forstag, D-Mont., as he headed to lunch after an orientation session on Monday.

Recent findings suggest that forstag is the first Democratic congressman from Montana in 30 years, succeeding retiring GOP Rep. Ryan Zinke. A former smokejumper who parachuted into remote forests to put out wildfires, Forstag won by more than 3 points in a district President Donald Trump carried by double digits in 2024.

Recent findings suggest that “I think there’s a lot of folks who didn’t expect us to,” he said of his win. “Nobody knew who we were this past December when I was still working at the smoke jumper base in Missoula.”.

Democrats are still digesting their larger-than-expected wins, which saw them flip more than 40 House seats and oust a number of high-profile incumbents, including National Republican Congressional Committee Chairman Richard Hudson, R-N.C.

Industry observers note that “It’s like drinking out of a firehose,” stated Rep.-elect Rebecca Cooke, D-Wis., who unseated incumbent GOP Rep. Derrick Van Orden in Wisconsin’s 3rd District.

Cooke and her opponent clashed during the campaign over his use of AI-generated ads that she described as deepfakes. Now, they have to work together to make sure the transition goes smoothly.

“The congressman said that he’s willing to be helpful in that transition. I think it’s notable that we make sure that the casework is transferred over, that constituent service is a priority, and that nothing falls through the cracks for people,” she said.

The 120th Congress will be full of history-makers, and a record-breaking number of women are set to serve in the House.

In a recent development, “This is a Congress with the most women ever to be a part of this chamber,” Cooke mentioned. “And a lot of [Democrats], frankly, from the Midwest, and so I’m excited to build that sort of power from the Midwest to make sure that our interests are represented.”.

The math isn’t lost on Republicans navigating a freshman class where they have fewer peers than they hoped.

Sources indicate that “I thought that it would probably go a little bit different. I think a lot of people did, but it is what it is. You work with what we have,” stated Rep.-elect Mark Lamb, R-Ariz.

But just like high school, everyone’s trying to make friends. As incoming members filed into the Capitol Visitor Center on Monday morning, Rep.-elect Cait Conley, D-N.Y., introduced herself to Rep.-elect Sydney Gruters, R-Fla.

Meanwhile, Rep.-elect Claire Valdez, D-N.Y., who describes herself as a “proud democratic socialist,” walked by chatting with Del.-elect Robert White, who will become only the third person in the modern era to hold the title of D.C.’s nonvoting delegate.

“I’m sitting next to a teacher right now; I’m sitting next to the mayor of Scranton … good, nice people,” noted Rep.-elect Zack Mullock, D-N.J., who said he was surprised by how many “regular people” he was meeting among the incoming class.

Rep.-elect Brad Lander, D-N.Y., who ousted fellow Democrat Dan Goldman in a Brooklyn-based primary before cruising to victory in the general election, was also making friends.

It has been revealed that “I was hanging out with Donavan McKinney yesterday in orientation, and I’m just really excited to meet all the amazing people. Micah Lasher, we were hanging out last night. Jacqui Irwin, so we’re just trying to get to know each other,” he said.

It has been revealed that after arriving on Sunday with suitcases in hand, the future freshmen got a chance to set foot inside the House chamber later that day. Lander said he’d been there before to see Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, a friend of his, get sworn in four years ago. But Sunday was his first time on the floor itself.

“It’s obviously a lot different when it’s you,” he said.

Koh agreed, saying “everyone in that room, Republican or Democrat, had a lot of reverence for where they were.”.

“I think it was just a good reminder about how despite all the division, that’s what we’re going to focus on — trying to figure out how to get things done for the American people,” he said.

Members-elect were trying their best to navigate their latest workplace on Monday, many of them donning backpacks as they came to terms with the realities of their new job.

“We just have to get back to class,” said Rep.-elect Ed Gallrein, R-Ky., to a crowd of reporters trying to flag him down as he left orientation to use the restroom.

They’d have Italian food for lunch, after a session in the CVC auditorium where many of the future members typed notes on their laptops.

In a recent development, “They’ve got a packed agenda for us all week, really helping us figure out how to get started. Build our team, set course, understand where the bathrooms are — large and small. We got a lot to learn,” Lander mentioned.

The libido drug women want is testosterone

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (633 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • These days, Jessica Yih spends a lot of time talking to women about testosterone.
  • It has been revealed that some non-hormonal treatments are now available, but the U.S.
  • Not many studies have looked at testosterone’s effects on libido in premenopausal women, but preliminary data in that area are also promising, according to a 2026 research review in The Journal of Sexual Medicine that Yih coauthored.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

These days, Jessica Yih spends a lot of time talking to women about testosterone. Interest is “coming from all directions,” says the University of California, Irvine Health urologist. A major source: women who hope testosterone can boost the female libido. Only about a decade ago, women looking for libido treatments had few medical options — even though women of all ages struggle with low sexual desire.

It has been revealed that some non-hormonal treatments are now available, but the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has yet to approve a female testosterone product, despite years of research suggesting it can boost sexual function and desire among postmenopausal women. Female testosterone products are approved in countries including the United Kingdom and Australia.

Not many studies have looked at testosterone’s effects on libido in premenopausal women, but preliminary data in that area are also promising, according to a 2026 research review in The Journal of Sexual Medicine that Yih coauthored. “I have seen it change people’s lives,” Yih says. The hormone seems to make the female brain more receptive to sexual stimuli; it also promotes physical effects that enhance sexual pleasure, such as increased blood flow to the genitals. Right now, American women interested in these potential benefits have to look for them off-label. But that may change. In September, the FDA held a public meeting on testosterone use among menopausal women, “with the goal of informing future research and potential drug development in this area,” says Kaveeta Vasisht, the FDA’s associate commissioner for women’s health.

In a recent development, the hormone has a rocky regulatory past. In 2004, an FDA advisory panel unanimously voted against approving a testosterone patch for women, citing a lack of safety data. There are still outstanding questions on that front, Yih claims—like how, if at all, long-term use affects risk of conditions such as breast cancer and heart disease. Then, in 2011, a pair of Phase III trials found that testosterone therapy didn’t significantly outperform a placebo — a benchmark the FDA looks for when deciding whether to approve a upcoming drug. That’s not to say testosterone didn’t work, says Tami Rowen, an ob-gyn at UC San Francisco. Rather, it seemed that hype about the hormone was so strong that study participants went in with sky-high expectations, leading even the placebo group to report benefits. The treatment was a “victim of its own success,” Rowen says.

Interest hasn’t let up, though. By one estimate, the U.S. female prescription rate for all uses rose from 0.4 out of every 1,000 women in 2018, to 1.8 out of every 1,000 women in 2026. That’s an increase of nearly 400 percent. With so much buzz, the potential placebo effect remains “the biggest problem with testosterone right now,” Rowen claims.

Another outstanding question, Yih says, is whether using testosterone long-term increases the risk of breast cancer and heart disease.

Women seeking a libido boost do have non-hormonal options. In 2015, the FDA approved Addyi, the first treatment for low libido in premenopausal women. The drug seemingly raises levels of neurotransmitters that promote sexual desire while tamping down those that block it. A competitor, Vyleesi, hit shelves in 2019. Then, last year, regulators expanded Addyi’s use to postmenopausal women younger than 65. An international group of experts, including Rowen, issued recommendations for treating low female libido in 2025 in Sexual Medicine Reviews. Psychological therapies and Addyi are backed by the strongest evidence, the group found.

In a recent development, rowen right now has her eye on in-development products including Lybrido. The drug, which is slated to enter a Phase III clinical trial in Europe, aims to rev sex drive in the brain and enhance physical arousal. The demand for newly introduced treatments is there, Rowen says. “Women deserve better than placebo.”.

#100090. Why does Webb see so many giant galaxies in the early universe?

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1101 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Why does Webb see so many giant galaxies in the early universe?

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1101 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Lumina simulation traces how stars and quasars transformed gas in the early universe and explores why Webb sees so many massive galaxies.
  • The first stars and galaxies gave off ultraviolet light that stripped electrons from hydrogen atoms between galaxies.
  • Quasars later began stripping helium of its last electron, a process that took more energetic light and was still underway long after most of the hydrogen had been ionized.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Lumina simulation traces how stars and quasars transformed gas in the early universe and explores why Webb sees so many massive galaxies.

The first stars and galaxies gave off ultraviolet light that stripped electrons from hydrogen atoms between galaxies.

Quasars later began stripping helium of its last electron, a process that took more energetic light and was still underway long after most of the hydrogen had been ionized.

A upcoming computer simulation called Lumina tracks how gas, dark matter and light interacted through both changes.

It models a region that would span about 1.6 billion light-years on each side at today’s cosmic scale, giving astronomers a way to test their predictions against observations from the James Webb Space Telescope.

Oliver Zier, a fellow at the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian, led the project.

Aaron Smith of the University of Texas at Dallas was a co-author, along with colleagues at MIT, York University and the Max Planck Institute for Astrophysics.

“With JWST, the early universe has become an exciting latest frontier in astrophysics,” Zier stated. “To understand what we are seeing with this telescope, we need to translate our theories into detailed predictions.”.

Sources indicate that A simulation is that translation. Astronomers feed in the laws of physics and the universe’s starting conditions, then let a supercomputer calculate how everything develops over time.

In a recent development, they compare the result with real telescope images. A match gives astronomers more confidence in the model. A mismatch can show where its assumptions need more testing.

Lumina covers roughly the first 2 billion years, following the earliest galaxies and the thin gas between them.

The simulated cube is about 1.6 billion light-years on a side, more than 100 times the volume of comparable simulations.

The team divided its contents into 432 billion pieces of gas and dark matter, and each piece of gas has about 3.6 million times the mass of the Sun.

Galaxies grow where the dark matter gathers, strung along the filaments of the cosmic web.

The team ran Lumina on Frontier, a supercomputer at Oak Ridge National Laboratory in Tennessee.

The simulation used 7,536 graphics accelerators, just over 20% of the machine, and about 600 terabytes of working memory at its peak.

Smith described what that size makes possible.

“For the first time, we can follow along as both hydrogen and helium changed into their modern form across such an enormous volume of the universe, while still resolving the galaxies and other luminous objects driving that transformation,” he remarked.

Earlier simulations of this kind, including the Thesan project, stopped before helium began to clear. Lumina’s cube is 144 times the volume of Thesan’s.

In a recent development, the first stars and galaxies cleared the hydrogen slowly and unevenly. In Lumina, bubbles of cleared gas open around the biggest galaxies first and grow until they merge. Regions far from any galaxy stay foggy longest.

The team divided the simulation into 125 regions and tracked how rapidly the hydrogen changed in each one.

Industry observers note that in a typical region, nearly all of the hydrogen gas between galaxies had lost its electrons by about 1.1 billion years after the Significant Bang. In the slowest regions, that took about 1.3 billion years.

Astronomers see the same late finish in the light of distant quasars, which still reveals absorption by hydrogen gas at that time.

Stars did nearly all of this work. Quasars supplied about 15% of the hydrogen-clearing light near the end.

Clearing helium takes light about four times more energetic than clearing hydrogen, and ordinary stars give off very little of it. Quasars do.

A quasar is a supermassive black hole pulling in gas so fast that the gas shines with intense ultraviolet light.

Sources indicate that in Lumina, the brightest quasars began stripping helium of its last electron about 900 million years after the Major Bang. The process was about halfway complete by 1.5 billion years.

By 2 billion years, the regions where helium still held its last electron accounted for less than 1% of the space Lumina modeled.

The bubbles around quasars grew larger than the hydrogen bubbles that formed around galaxies.

Each clearing also heats the gas. The thin gas between galaxies warms to roughly 18,000°F to 36,000°F (10,000°C to 20,000°C) while the hydrogen clears.

It cools as the universe expands, then warms again when the quasar light reaches it.

Sources indicate that measurements of the helium clearing are scarce. Most studies of it rely on fewer than about 25 quasars with a usable line of sight, and Lumina’s timing agrees with those measurements.

Lumina also grows galaxies, and here it fails a test. At about 1.2 billion years after the Substantial Bang and earlier, the simulation produces fewer very massive galaxies than Webb has found.

The shortfall grows the further back in time the comparison goes.

The team wrote that this confirms a known problem: galaxy models tuned to the nearby universe undercount the giants Webb sees in the early one.

Stars might form more efficiently in the earliest big galaxies, or the masses astronomers read off Webb’s images might be less certain than assumed.

The simulation can’t settle that on its own, but it marks where the standard picture falls short.

Some of Lumina’s agreement with observations is built in.

The authors set the share of each galaxy’s hydrogen-clearing light that escapes into space at 18%, a value chosen so that hydrogen clears on a realistic schedule. So the timing of that clearing is partly a tuning choice, not a prediction.

The team also slowed the speed of light in the calculation to a fifth of its real value, because the full speed would have made the run unaffordable.

Sources indicate that that shortcut may keep hydrogen fog in remote voids a little too long. And the detailed comparison with real quasar spectra, the one that would say whether the helium timing is right, is still to come.

It has been revealed that zier’s team intends to release the full Lumina data in 2028. Companion studies are already using it to work out how patchy clearing marks the afterglow of the Significant Bang, and how many quasars of each brightness the early universe held.

Observations from Webb and future surveys by the Roman Space Telescope will help astronomers test whether Lumina can explain how the earliest massive galaxies formed.

The full study was published in the journal Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Industry observers note that unlike window air conditioners, portable air conditioners roll easily from room to room and take only minutes to set up—no brackets, no tools, no sweating through a complicated installation before you can start sweating less. Most just require a nearby window and wall outlet to get cold air flowing. Yes, they tend to cost a bit more than window units, but the tradeoff is real: you can’t beat the convenience their portability adds, which is why many people choose them over other models. Plus your view isn’t blocked by a giant metal box.

Portable air conditioners have an internal fan that moves hot, humid air over a refrigerant-gas-filled coil to cool and expel it into a room to lower the temperature. The moisture it strips from the air collects in an internal reservoir that you’ll periodically need to drain. Higher-end units either pump it out automatically or evaporate it entirely so you never have to think about it. Because the whole unit rolls on casters, you can take the cold air with you instead of running more energy intensive central a/c or buying multiple window units.

In a recent development, to find the best models to recommend, we tested air conditioners from trusted brands like LG, GE, Black + Decker, Midea, Hisense, and more. These are the units that stood out and are worth the investment.

We placed each unit in its own room and directed its discharge hose to the outside, then set the appliance’s temperature to 68 degrees and its fan speed to maximum. We directed the cold air each unit discharged at a target 8 feet away, then used an infrared thermometer to measure the temperature at four different locations on the target. We also checked the appliance’s outlet to see if it maintained a consistent temperature. To test the wheels’ durability and noise, we rolled each unit on a hard surface to maximize squeaks and rattles.

Sources indicate that we also sent several air conditioners to our staff’s homes and apartments for further testing, where our editors used them over the course of weeks within the living spaces. We tested how easy they were to use, how they operated over time, and how easy they were to integrate into daily life.

For our most recent revision, we identified the most trusted brands and surveyed current models across a range of price points, BTU capacities, and capabilities, making sure we had options for small rooms and larger ones. From there, we narrowed the field by prioritizing units with strong efficiency ratings, straightforward setup, and drainage designs that won’t require constant attention.

Industry observers note that our top-rated portable air conditioner stands out for how rapidly it cools down a room. During testing, we turned it on and almost immediately began feeling a cold blast of air with very little runtime. The a/c noticeably brought down the temperature in just a few minutes, plus it did so quietly. According to LG, the unit operates at just 44 decibels on its lowest setting.

In a recent development, the unit has three modes: cooling, fan, and dry. Cooling and fan are pretty straightforward while dry actually turns the unit into a dehumidifier. So, when you don’t actively need it, feel free to have it run in moist spaces like your laundry room or garage.

The louvers on the a/c unit can be set to move up and down on their own. This actually made a pretty notable difference in full-room air circulation and helped get rid of hot air that sat near the ceiling.

Setup was also quite easy, as the air conditioner was almost fully assembled right out of the box. Even connecting the hose and slider into the window was intuitive and took less than 5 minutes total. With the four wheels and very basic setup, we were rolling it from room to room in no time.

Full LG Portable Air Conditioner Review.

If you’re hesitant to spend over $500 on a portable air conditioning unit, this option from Dreo is the best bang for your buck. Considering the relatively low price, its power and added features surprised us during testing.

First and foremost, the unit blasts cold air quite rapidly. In fact, it worked nearly as well as several of the more expensive units we tested. The window exhaust has a foam seal to make sure no hot exhaust or exterior air sneaks in.

The air conditioner pairs with Dreo’s app for connection and precise programming, however we ended up using (and loving) the physical remote. It has 10 buttons for changing the speed and temperature, setting the air mode, operating the sleep timer, turning on the auto-swing louver function, and more. Plus, there’s an attached magnet for convent storage on top of the unit.

In a recent development, on the front of the unit there are manual controls and a digital display that shows the room temperature, mode, and fan power. So whether you’re using the remote, app, or changing settings manually, you know exactly what the status is.

Full Dreo AC515S Portable Air Conditioner Review.

It has been revealed that this Whynter’s amperage and BTU capacity position it firmly in the heavy-duty cooling category. The same applies to its dehumidifying power, with the unit capturing up to 71 pints of moisture per day. The biggest downside is that it’s also firmly in the heavy category, weighing over 70 pounds.

The portable air conditioner has a dual-hose design (intake and exhaust) for reducing the amount of condensate that the a/c collects, since it’s supposed to be removed in the exhaust air stream.

A similar model (ARC-14SH) also operates in heat pump/heater mode. For a slightly smaller model, check out the Whynter Elite ARC-122DS below.

While most units are either quiet or powerful, the GE Profile Portable A/C offers a bit of both worlds. Because of its dual-hose design, the air conditioner takes in air at a much higher rate than one that relies on the body of the unit to do this work. With more air coming in, more cold air comes out. This was definitely true during testing.

It has been revealed that on its average setting, the a/c noticeably cooled down a mid-sized room in less than ten minutes. Holding up my hand to the vents, I felt a cold blast of air much stronger than other options I tried out. Going even further, the Profile has a turbo mode that turns the fans up to an even higher level.

The effectiveness of the cooling has do to with more than just airflow, too. This portable a/c unit also comes with auto louvers that more evenly distribute cold air by shifting the vents up and down. I particularly like this feature for apartments like mine which are a few floors up and end up with a lot of accumulated hot air near the ceiling. The auto louvers help bring down the temperature of the entire room down as opposed to just blasting cold air in one direction.

Recent findings suggest that while all these features impressed me, the unit’s best quality is that it doesn’t stand out at all. This a/c is incredibly quiet. While I barely noticed the sound at normal levels, when I set the unit to quiet mode, the noise levels drop to a whisper. According to GE, quiet mode is measured at just 42 decibels, which is lower than all other options we recommend.

Recent findings suggest that this makes the Profile an ideal choice for overnight use or in small rooms. However, the remote control buttons don’t light up, so if you’re using it at night, you may need a flashlight, phone, or bedside lamp.

Full GE Profile Portable Air Conditioner Review.

If the other units on this list take up more real estate than you have or want to give, the Dreo AC319S is the one you won’t have to make room for. It's the most compact refrigerant-based portable air conditioner we've included—at just over 17 inches wide and 28 inches tall, it slips into corners and tight apartments where bulkier units don't fit. Be warned, though, the tradeoff for that smaller footprint is smaller cooling coverage. This one is best for bedrooms, home offices, and other spaces up to 300 square feet.

But what it gives up in cooling-size capabilities, it makes up for in smart features and low maintenance. The drainage-free system, powered by Dreo's patented internal pump and dual water sensors, handles condensation automatically. In moderately humid conditions, you'll likely never need to drain the unit at all. The Dreo app sends a notification if the tank does fill up, which is a thoughtful touch. That kind of hands-off convenience is why this one made our list.

Sources indicate that at just 45 decibels on its lowest setting, it's whisper-quiet on par with the priciest units here. Smart controls are also unusually comprehensive. In addition to Alexa and Google Assistant, the AC319S works with Siri, making it one of the only portable ACs that pairs nicely with Apple products. The circular LED display looks sharp, though you can’t dim it, so keep that in mind if you strategy to use it overnight in rooms you want to stay dark.

Sources indicate that if you’re fortunate to have a large living room, an open-blueprint studio, or a finished basement, you know the luxury of size comes with a cost—cooling oversized areas can be tough. To beat the heat in significant rooms, the Whynter ARC-1230WN is the unit we’d point you toward.

With 14,000 BTUs, it covers up to 600 square feet—more than any other unit on this list. In independent testing, it dropped room temperature by about 12 degrees in a single hour, a result no other unit came close to matching.

According to recent reports, A significant part of that performance comes from Whynter's hose-in-hose dual-hose design. Unlike a standard dual-hose setup, the intake and exhaust lines run concentrically inside a single tube, preventing heat leakage between the airstreams and improving overall efficiency. The inverter compressor, which ramps up and down rather than cycling on and off, keeps noise down once the room reaches your set temperature and reduces energy use.

In a recent development, according to Whynter, the inverter technology delivers 20 percent more cooling capacity and over 40 percent energy savings compared to non-inverter models. Do note, though, that while this is technically a portable unit, at more than 75 pounds, it’s one you’ll want to set up for the season, not haul around on the regular.

If you're shopping for a portable AC because you have a room your HVAC system can’t handle, the Midea Duo MAP14HS1TBL is our top recommendation. It's a four-season unit: the same inverter-driven, hose-in-hose dual-hose design that makes it such an effective cooler works equally well in heat mode, and switching between the two is as easy as a click on the remote or SmartHome app—no setup or adjustments required.

It has been revealed that the dual-hose design pulls in fresh air and expels exhaust air through a single concentric hose, keeping a neutral pressure balance in rooms. This prevents warm outside air from coming back in through gaps and cracks. Midea's airflow system also projects air up to 26 feet, which makes a real difference in longer rooms where less forceful units only cool the area immediately around them.

We’re also impressed by the smart controls. The SmartHome app works on iOS, Android, and Apple Watch, and voice control is compatible with Alexa and Google Assistant. I also like that you can completely turn off the control panel lights, which is a sleep-saving feature for overnight use. And at 42 decibels on its lowest setting, it's among the quietest options we’ve come across.

Industry observers note that we were pleasantly surprised by the power and value offered by this small portable air conditioner from Black+Decker. It begins producing cold air very swiftly, though not quite at the volume of many other air conditioners we tested. That noted, it still reduced the temperature of its target at a rapid rate.

The unit provides multiple fan speeds, dedicated dehumidification, a timer setting, and a sleep setting. Note that there is no heater setting on this appliance. It’s meant to cool and dehumidify exclusively.

Reviews Editor Amber Joglar tested out the four-in-one version of this model which also functions as a heater. After just 10 minutes of use in her room, Joglar felt, “a noticeable shift in the air temperature.”.

The quick cooldown times stood out across both models, though Joglar also pointed out that this led to the exhaust pipes heating up swiftly as well. This isn’t necessarily a problem, but if you plan on using the unit for several hours a day, consider covering the tubes in insulation.

In addition to the cold air, Joglar liked the remote and LED control panel, saying, “I normally just change settings on the air conditioner itself because it’s right next to my bed, so backlit controls are helpful.”.

Similarly, the remote control is great for when she’s already in bed or wants to pre-cool the room before she’s ready to go to sleep.

Joglar’s model also heats rooms. So, instead of storing it in a closet or attic for the cold winter months, she simply switches functionality.

Read Our Full Black+Decker Portable Air Conditioner Review.

Coverage area is one of the most important factors in choosing an air conditioner. Manufacturers rate units in square footage, but that number assumes an average ceiling height (roughly eight feet) and room insulation. If the room is especially hot in the summer (for example, it’s a finished attic or it has large, south-facing windows) we recommend bumping up to the next size rather than buying a unit that will run constantly and struggle to keep up.

Industry observers note that an air conditioner’s cooling capacity is typically measured in British Thermal Units, or BTU, per hour. To gauge coverage, figure roughly 20 BTU per square foot of space. Most portable a/c units range from 5,000 to 20,000 BTUs, which puts their effective range roughly between 350 and 700 square feet. So when in doubt, size up—an oversized unit cycles off when it hits your target temperature, while an undersized one never stops trying.

According to recent reports, single-hose units essentially recirculate the room’s air to cool it and have one line that runs outdoors to expel exhaust. The catch is that expelling air creates a slight negative pressure in the room, which pulls in warm air from other parts of the house and from outside through gaps around doors and windows. It works, but it’s working against itself.

Industry observers note that dual-hose units solve this by pulling outside air in through one hose for cooling and pushing hot exhaust out through a second hose. The result is a more self-contained system that’s noticeably more efficient, especially in larger spaces. The tradeoff is price.

In a recent development, because dual-hose models are more complex, they tend to be more expensive. If you only have a small space to cool, a portable a/c with a single hose may suit your needs just fine. For anything larger, the dual-hose design is worth seriously considering.

Hose length determines how far away from a window you can maneuver your portable air conditioner. If you set it up in a large room, or one where the nearest window is far from where most people gather, hose length becomes more important.

It also plays a key role in room setup. If the hose isn’t long enough to set the air conditioner in front of large furniture pieces, you may have to rearrange the room for the most effective cooling. Most hoses range anywhere from 50 to 90 inches fully extended. This should give you enough space to make adjustments and pull the air conditioner closer to the center of the room if needed.

Industry observers note that most portable air conditioners hover between 50 and 60 decibels while they’re running—that’s roughly the noise level of a normal conversation. In most cases, that’s fine during the day, but if you’re planning to run the unit in a bedroom overnight, those numbers start to matter.

Units that dip below 50 decibels in their quietest modes are on par with most ceiling fans and are easier to sleep through; a few on this list get impressively close to whisper-quiet. Pay attention to the decibel rating at the unit’s lowest fan setting, not just its average operating level.

It has been revealed that much like larger ductless mini-split air conditioners, some portable air conditioners include a heat pump. “If you’re shopping for an a/c unit because you have a space not at the moment cooled or heated, one of these models may warrant consideration,” states gear editor Bradley Ford. “Similarly, you may have a room that your HVAC system doesn’t reach effectively. Rooms like this are typically either too cold or hot, depending on the season. If this is the case, a unit with heating capabilities may be able to fill your HVAC gap.”.

Every portable a/c pulls moisture out of the air, similar to home dehumidifiers. The question is what happens to it next. Budget units collect it in an internal pan that you’ll need to manually drain, sometimes daily in humid conditions.

Other units use self-evaporating technology to push moisture out through the exhaust hose with no bucket to remember. A few high-end models go even further, offering a continuous drainage port where you can attach a hose and never think about water again. If low-maintenance matters to you, the drainage method is a factor to consider.

According to recent reports, there isn’t a clear superior option between window units and portable options. Choosing between the two largely depends on your home, windows, and personal needs. That mentioned, window air conditioning units are generally faster at bringing temperatures down and run more efficiently than their portable counterparts.

Portable air conditioners have certainly closed the gap over time in terms of cooling ability, but still lag behind if that’s your number one priority.

Recent findings suggest that portable units stand out because of their convenience and ease of setup. If you don’t have compatible windows, get a portable unit. If you need quick cooling in a spot that generally doesn’t need air conditioning, get a portable unit. If you want just one machine for your entire apartment, get a portable unit.

Portable air conditioners are compatible with a lot more window openings than window units, so you can use them regardless of your apartment or home fixtures.

New portable a/c units are relatively energy efficient across the board. That remarked, it’s certainly a sliding scale. There are several ways in which energy efficiency is calculated for air conditioners, but the shorthand is if your a/c unit is Energy Star-certified, it’s worth getting.

For items that don’t have Energy Star certification, pay attention to the CEER, EER, and SEER numbers. In short, look for an air conditioner with a CEER above 10, with anything above 12 qualifying for Energy Star certification. Similarly, look out for a SEER above 14 in the north and 15 in the south as well as an EER above 10. These are general numbers, but serve as a basic guide when choosing between different options.

Recent findings suggest that one of the biggest issues to solve with portable air conditioners is cooling efficiency. While most units generate a ton of cold air, leakage from the hose or exhaust port can work against that. There are two key things you can do: insulate the opening in the window and insulate the hose itself.

Many portable units provide foam pieces that fit in and around the window insert to minimize the amount of hot air that leaks in from outside. The hose itself won’t come with foam insulation pieces, but you can perform a similar trick by buying one online or by making one yourself. Some people use blankets while others have used everything from reflective sun shades to Amazon plastic packaging. The goal is to prevent heat from the tube from radiating into your living space.

#100088. The wildlife trade is bigger than previously thought, with nearly 80,000 species and counting

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1375 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

The wildlife trade is bigger than previously thought, with nearly 80,000 species and counting

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1375 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A new review finds that global wildlife trade reaches far beyond familiar pets and seafood, and gaps in recordkeeping make its full scale hard to measure.
  • Ask about the wildlife trade and most people picture smuggled ivory, tiger skins and pangolins.
  • Most documented wildlife trade is legal, and it includes the fish in the freezer aisle, the orchid on the windowsill, and the gecko in the pet shop window.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A new review finds that global wildlife trade reaches far beyond familiar pets and seafood, and gaps in recordkeeping make its full scale hard to measure.

Ask about the wildlife trade and most people picture smuggled ivory, tiger skins and pangolins. Almost none of the recorded trade is like that.

Most documented wildlife trade is legal, and it includes the fish in the freezer aisle, the orchid on the windowsill, and the gecko in the pet shop window.

A upcoming review documented 79,554 species in international wildlife trade, well above the roughly 50,000 previously estimated.

A broader tally that included species people use for subsistence and other purposes reached 107,356.

Even the new number is likely a considerable underestimate, the authors wrote, because almost no country records what it buys and sells.

According to recent reports, alice Hughes, a conservation scientist at the University of Melbourne, led the review. Her co-authors come from the organizations that track wildlife trade, including TRAFFIC, the IUCN and the UN’s Food and Agriculture Organization.

The count comes from stitching together databases built for other purposes, and the plant half of it rests on records of use rather than records of sale.

In an interview with Earth.com, Hughes said the finding is about ordinary buyers as much as smugglers.

“Almost all of us are part of wildlife trade, and whilst some of that, such as fisheries are managed, sectors like the pet trade are not,” she said.

Recent findings suggest that legal wildlife trade is worth an estimated $220 billion to $300 billion a year. Smuggled wildlife is worth an estimated $28 billion to $40 billion.

So the legal side is roughly six to 11 times larger than the smuggling that gets the attention.

“When we think of wildlife trade we tend to think about the illegal trade of elephants, tigers and pangolins. But it’s much more than that,” Hughes mentioned.

“Wildlife trade includes everything from timber, seafood and medicinal plants to pets, cut flowers, ornamental fish and fungi, and most of it is legal.”.

According to recent reports, legal doesn’t mean harmless. Where researchers have population numbers for a traded species, the populations being collected from are, on average, 50% to 60% smaller than populations left alone.

By one estimate the authors cite, trade has contributed, directly or indirectly, to the global extinction of 294 species.

The team pulled together every trade record it could reach. The largest was the CITES Trade Database, which holds the records of legal trade in protected species going back to 1975.

Alongside it went the IUCN Red List, UN fish and timber records, TRAFFIC’s seizure reports and the US import database.

Beyond the databases, the researchers drew on published surveys of individual animal groups and a world checklist of plants that people use.

Recent findings suggest that animals accounted for 47,685 species, and up to 31,306 of those are vertebrates. That works out to 42% of every vertebrate species science has described.

Put another way, two out of every five kinds of animal with a backbone have been traded somewhere.

Sources indicate that for birds, the share is higher still: about 65% of all living bird species have been traded. Plants and fungi added 59,671 species potentially used or traded.

According to recent reports, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service logs wild animal shipments into and out of the United States in a database called LEMIS, and it periodically releases the records.

Since 2000, more than 21,000 wild animal species have been traded into the US alone.

Recent findings suggest that more than a quarter of all traded animal species appear in that one country’s records and in no other database. For mammals, the figure is 54%.

Much of what the world knows about which animals are traded comes from one country’s import records.

Recent findings suggest that hughes’s team surveyed 61 countries and searched for “wildlife trade database” in 30 languages. The US system was the only full, public record of trade across groups of animals from any country.

Sources indicate that “The United States is the only country that systematically records and publicly shares trade data across a wide range of taxa. For much of the rest of the world, equivalent data simply does not exist,” Hughes remarked.

Asked what it would take for other countries to follow, Hughes told Earth.com it starts with accepting that “legal trade is not necessarily sustainable.”.

Without data on trade in other groups, she said, the trade can’t be managed to make sure it is sustainable.

“Trade has changed, the exotic pet trade will continue to grow, and with so many species in trade, that poses a real risk unless we start monitoring it better,” she mentioned.

Sources indicate that the pet trade is where the fresh counts diverge most from the old global estimates. The gaps are largest for reptiles, invertebrates and plants, which are also the hardest to track.

A lizard or a beetle bought online travels by mail and often isn’t identified to species at the border.

CITES, the treaty that regulates trade in at-risk species, covers about 9.5% of reptile species. The new review recorded 4,620 reptile species in trade, about 37% of all described reptiles.

Asked which traded species surprised her most, Hughes stated it was how promptly newly described species appear for sale.

Sources indicate that collectors sometimes use the scientific descriptions themselves to find animals to trade, she noted. She also pointed to “the price people are willing to pay for some, like 100s of dollars for a single isopod (woodlouse).”.

For buyers, Hughes mentioned the place to start is where an animal came from.

Corn snakes and leopard geckos should be captive bred, she noted, and chameleons often come from the wild and don’t survive well in captivity.

“If you are not sure where they come from, just don’t buy them, for every wild caught animal in the shop, many others die in transit,” she said.

Governments have agreed on a set of global biodiversity targets, and one of them covers the impacts of trade.

Its single headline measure is the share of fish stocks being fished at sustainable levels. By the review’s count, that measure reflects about 2% of the species in use and trade.

“While the global biodiversity framework does have a target on trade, based on our estimates it only accounts for around two or three percent of species in trade and misses the other 97 percent,” Hughes said.

In a recent development, the authors wrote that the fix doesn’t need a latest system. Almost every country already runs customs checks and animal health checks on imports, and most CITES permits are still paper.

Electronic permits exist, but only about 30 of the 184 CITES countries use them.

If customs offices digitized shipping invoices and matched them to a species list, the authors wrote, they would record much of what is now lost.

The United Kingdom has required an electronic tag on every sheep, and a log of its movements, since 2009, so record-keeping on that scale is already being done.

Seizure records reflect how hard a country enforces its laws as much as how much is smuggled. And the databases don’t agree with one another on which species are traded, which is part of the paper’s point.

Even so, Hughes said the estimate is still an underestimate, because most countries do not collect the data.

The larger question is whether wild populations can sustain the trade. An IUCN working group has assessed the potential sustainability of trade for 347 species across 117 countries.

For many traded species, researchers still lack the data to tell how much is being taken from the wild and how those populations are faring.

Hughes and her co-authors propose standardizing how trade data are collected and starting at a regional level, with the European Union as a possible first model.

Until that happens, each fresh database that opens is likely to add species to the count.

For many species, researchers still can’t tell how trade is affecting wild populations.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.

#100086. Redistricting battle could spill into 2028

Redistricting battle could spill into 2028

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (946 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, maryland Gov.
  • The redistricting fights that underscored this year’s battle for the House could continue into the 2028 election cycle, although lessons from last Tuesday will likely shape those efforts.
  • House Republicans had hoped that newly introduced congressional maps in seven states would help them limit losses in the face of an unfavorable political environment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, maryland Gov. Wes Moore, here at the Capitol in January, wants to see his state's congressional map redrawn. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

The redistricting fights that underscored this year’s battle for the House could continue into the 2028 election cycle, although lessons from last Tuesday will likely shape those efforts.

House Republicans had hoped that newly introduced congressional maps in seven states would help them limit losses in the face of an unfavorable political environment. But nearly a week after the election, the GOP appeared on track to flip just three redrawn seats while losing a host of seats in Texas, Florida, North Carolina, Ohio and Alabama that were reconfigured in their favor.

“The question is whether the results have let some air out of the [redistricting] balloon or not,” mentioned Erik Nisbet, a professor at Northwestern University’s School of Communication.

Sources indicate that republicans may question the utility of redrawing more state maps in the 2028 cycle, while Democrats will need to weigh how to spend their political capital. But the latest lines approved over the past year could still prove more favorable for Republicans in future elections.

“This was a wave election, and there’s no guarantee that the Democratic generic ballot would be D+13 — which is the reason why redistricting didn’t work for Republicans — in the next cycle,” Nisbet added.

Latest maps appear possible, if not likely, in at least a few states. Maryland voters last week approved an amendment that would clear the way for new boundaries ahead of the 2028 elections. Democratic Gov. Wes Moore, who easily won a second term last week, mentioned he hopes to see a new map, citing the threat of President Donald Trump continuing to push for friendlier lines in GOP-led states. Maryland Democrats could draw a map that would favor them in all eight of the state’s House seats, including the Eastern Shore district of Rep. Andy Harris, the state’s lone Republican in Congress.

In a recent development, advocates for a new map in Wisconsin got a boost last week when Democrats flipped both the state House and state Senate, setting up a Democratic trifecta. Gov.-elect David Crowley said he would sign a bill redrawing the state’s congressional map if legislators sent one to his desk.

Republicans in recent years have had a lopsided edge in the congressional delegation for Wisconsin, a perennial battleground state. But Democrats flipped two House seats last week, with Rebecca Cooke and Mitchell Berman unseating GOP Reps. Derrick Van Orden and Bryan Steil, respectively, bringing the state delegation to an even 4-4.

Democrats could also look to redraw the lines in Upcoming York and Virginia. Earlier this year, voters in the commonwealth approved a new map that would have given Democrats up to four pickup opportunities, but the Virginia Supreme Court later struck it down on procedural grounds. Even without the new map, Democrats flipped two House seats in Virginia last week and came within 2 points of flipping a third.

Democrats in Newly introduced York, meanwhile, took initial steps toward mid-decade redistricting earlier this year, but 2028 is the earliest they could hold elections under a new map.

On the Republican side, several states have been mentioned as candidates for latest maps in 2028.

Officials in GOP-led Mississippi have held hearings this year on redistricting, which could target Democratic Rep. Bennie Thompson. Republicans are also aiming to redraw the state’s legislative lines ahead of next year’s off-year elections.

It’s not clear whether states that were unsuccessful in redrawing their district lines for 2026 will try again when their legislatures convene next year. Republicans in both South Carolina and Indiana fell short in their push to pass newly introduced maps and could decide to revisit the glitch. But Democrats flipped a House seat in each state last week, and some Republican incumbents won reelection by narrower margins than usual. Still, Republicans maintained their legislative majorities in both states, though Democrats broke their supermajorities in the South Carolina and Indiana state houses.

An analysis by DecisionDeskHQ offers a potential warning sign for Republicans in the Palmetto and Hoosier states: Under the GOP-drawn maps that were not adopted for 2026, Democrats could have flipped even more seats last week.

Redistricting appears off the table in a handful of states where fresh maps for 2028 had once been considered possible.

Georgia’s outgoing Republican governor, Brian Kemp, stated last week that he would not call a special session to address redistricting before the end of the year, after Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms was elected to succeed him.

There were no House flips in the Peach State in the midterm elections, though several Republicans won by closer-than-anticipated margins.

Sources indicate that in Fresh Jersey, Democratic Gov. Mikie Sherrill told the New Jersey Globe that she also did not “see a path forward for redistricting right now.”.

In a recent development, democrats flipped two House seats in the Garden State last week. Navy veteran Rebecca Bennett defeated Republican Rep. Thomas H. Kean Jr., while Cape May Mayor Zack Mullock scored a surprise win over GOP Rep. Jeff Van Drew.

With their upcoming majorities in Washington, Democrats could propose legislation to ban partisan gerrymandering.

That’s something John Bisognano, the president of the National Democratic Redistricting Committee, anticipates happening, but he mentioned Democrat-led states should be prepared to respond to latest maps drawn in Republican-controlled ones.

“If they are going to continue to take those actions, Democrats in states across the country need to be prepared to respond, and we, of course, now have significantly more opportunities than we did before Tuesday to respond to those states,” he said.
